archetypes.title: Agent-to-agent federation across platforms
summary: Our agent working with agents other organisations run — a vendor platform's agent, a partner's — over the Agent2Agent protocol, in both directions. The whole architecture is an identity problem: which agent is speaking, on whose behalf, with what it may do, and how far that authority is allowed to travel.
description:
A2A is thin on purpose. It defines how agents discover each other (a signed Agent Card), how they exchange work (tasks, messages, artifacts, over gRPC, HTTP+JSON or JSON-RPC) and which authentication schemes a peer accepts — and it stops there. Credentials are obtained out of band; the identity that authenticates is the calling agent, not the user it works for; whether a card is signed is a MAY; per-skill authorization is delegated to whatever sits in front of the agent. Everything an enterprise needs for identity is therefore plumbing it brings itself, and this drawing is that plumbing, made explicit: workload identities for agents, identity assertions for users, an authorization server that mints and exchanges, and a gateway that admits cards and enforces scopes per skill.
Two identities travel on every task and must never be confused. The agent's identity says which workload is calling — our harness registered as a client in the peer's platform, the peer's agent registered in ours — authenticated with a private key or mutual TLS, never a shared secret. The user's identity says on whose behalf, and it travels as an identity assertion the peer's platform can verify because it federates with our identity provider, exchanged for a token whose audience is that peer and whose scope is the skill being invoked. Where no federation exists, the user's identity does not travel at all: the task stops in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` and the person authenticates to the peer themselves.
Authority must not propagate. A token our gateway obtains for a peer is bound to that peer and to one skill; when the peer delegates onward to a third agent, it does so on its own identity and whatever grant its user gave it, not on ours — the delegation-chain opacity that OWASP names is exactly this token travelling one hop too far. Inbound, the same rule: a peer's token is accepted only if its audience is our agent, validated on every request, and never forwarded to our tool servers or systems of record, which are reached on a token exchanged for the purpose.
Everything a peer returns is untrusted content read by our model. Artifacts, status messages and the card itself land in our agent's context as instruction, so the gateway classifies inbound artifacts the way it classifies any tool result, and the card a peer publishes is admitted once — signature verified, hash pinned, skills reviewed — into a registry our agents may reach, not discovered live from the open web.
How much of this is in production is an honest question. A2A reached 1.0 in March 2026 under the Agentic AI Foundation, the specification has three formal bindings, and the major agent platforms publish cards; but most enterprise agent networks today are internal, and cross-organisation federation is early. This drawing is the target state to build toward and the checklist to hold a vendor's A2A story against, not a claim about what is common.
distinguishedBy:
Against the multi-agent workflow: there the specialists are ours, in one harness, on one identity, and the delegation chain is internal. Here every hop crosses an organisation, and what was a function call becomes an authenticated request with a scope.
Against the remote MCP server we publish: the same authorization machinery — an authorization server, audience-bound tokens, identity assertions — pointed at a peer that is an agent rather than a tool. The difference is that a peer acts, delegates onward and returns content composed by a model, so the artifact path and the delegation chain need controls a tool result never did.
Against the enterprise AI chat with connectors: there the vendor's agent reaches into our systems through our gateway as a tool caller. Here two agents negotiate work as peers, in both directions, and each side is somebody's published agent.

exemplars.name: Agent2Agent protocol v1.0
exemplars.note: The specification this drawing follows — signed Agent Cards (JWS over a canonical form), the A2A-Version header, three bindings, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect and mutual TLS as the declared security schemes, and the auth-required task state.

exemplars.name: Enterprise agent platforms with A2A endpoints
exemplars.note: The major agent platforms publish Agent Cards and accept tasks over A2A; each brings its own authorization server and tenant model, which is why the token endpoint is an item on the peer and why federation is decided per platform.

exemplars.name: Identity assertion authorization grant
exemplars.note: The IETF draft that gives a user's identity a way to travel between an identity provider and another organisation's authorization server without a browser — the same mechanism enterprise-managed authorization uses for MCP, applied here to a peer agent's token endpoint.

zones.note: The person whose task crosses to another organisation's agent — present at the start, and asked again only when a peer needs their own consent.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the surface that binds the user's identity, our identity provider and authorization server, the harness that speaks A2A in both directions, the crossing every task leaves and arrives through, and our own tool servers and systems of record.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: An agent platform we hold an agreement with. Its agent, its Agent Card, its token endpoint and its tenant model are theirs; what we hold is the assessment behind the agreement and the federation that lets our users' identity be honoured there.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: Outside any agreement: the model provider our harness infers on, and a partner organisation's agent that ours works with on nothing more than a signed card and a registration.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band: the identities of our agents, the registry of peers we admit, the per-skill policy the gateway enforces, and the audit that has to join two organisations' records on one task.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: The person on whose behalf the task runs. Their identity is the thing that must travel to the peer correctly — or not travel, and be asked for again.

blocks.title: Identity provider
blocks.note: Our identity provider, drawn because tokens flow through it: the user signs in here, the front end holds the resulting ID token, and the authorization server turns that login into identity assertions a federated peer platform will honour. Federation is a relationship configured here, per platform — the peer's token endpoint trusts our issuer and keys, or it does not, and that decides which of the two user-identity walks applies.

items.label: SSO login
items.note: The corporate sign-in; its ID token is the subject token for every exchange that follows.

items.label: Token exchange
items.note: RFC 8693 in our own house: the user's login exchanged for an assertion whose audience is a specific peer platform's authorization server, carrying the user's `sub` and the skill scope requested — never a broad token.

items.label: App registry & policy
items.note: Which peer platforms our users' identity may be asserted to, and for whom. Removing a group ends every new assertion to that peer at once.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: Where the user's identity is bound before anything is delegated. Drawn because the user is the core input here — a task that will travel between organisations starts with a person asking for it — and because the auth-required round trip returns here.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published surface the user's request arrives on.

items.label: Identity binding
items.note: Who is asking, bound at the start; the identity every downstream assertion is about, and the thing a peer will be told.

blocks.title: Authorization server
blocks.note: Ours, and the hinge of the drawing in both directions. Outbound it exchanges the user's login for an identity assertion aimed at a peer platform, and holds our harness's own client credentials for each peer — a private key per registration, never a shared secret. Inbound it is the token endpoint our published Agent Card names: a peer agent authenticates here with its registered identity and receives a token whose audience is our agent and whose scopes are the skills that peer was admitted for, and the gateway asks it to validate every request and to mint the downstream tokens our tools are reached with.

items.label: Token issuance
items.note: Audience-bound to one agent, scoped to named skills, short-lived.

items.label: Grant profiles
items.note: `client_credentials` with `private_key_jwt` or mutual TLS for agent identities; the JWT-bearer grant for a federated peer's user assertions; token exchange for on-behalf-of tokens outbound and downstream. Nothing interactive unless a person is genuinely present.

items.label: Client registration
items.note: Each peer agent we admit is a registered client with its own key; each peer platform we call has registered ours. Registration is where an agent gets an identity, and deregistration is where it loses one.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: Our agent, speaking A2A both ways: a client that delegates a slice of the user's task to a peer, and a server whose signed Agent Card other organisations' agents discover and call. It holds no credentials for peers itself — the gateway obtains them — and it treats what peers return as content, not instruction.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides which part of the task a peer should do, and reads what comes back as one more input.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the request, memory and every artifact a peer returned into one prompt.

items.label: A2A client
items.note: Sends tasks and reads artifacts, streams or polls, sends `A2A-Version`, and hands the peer's `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` back to the person rather than guessing.

items.label: Agent card
items.note: Our published card: skills, the security schemes we accept (OAuth 2.0 against our authorization server, mutual TLS inside a trust boundary), our push-notification expectations — signed, with the key discoverable, because a card that can be tampered with redirects every caller.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The harness's built-in tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop. Here they matter for one reason: memory, where a peer's artifact would persist if it were written unclassified.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Functions in the application, including the state and retrieval reads the loop treats as context.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Task state across the days a federated task may take, and the artifacts peers returned. Anything written here from a peer is prose the next turn treats as instruction.

items.label: Case state
items.note: Which peer holds which slice, and the task ids to reconcile against.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Retrieval over past artifacts — the poisoning surface if artifacts are stored unclassified.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The crossing every task leaves and arrives through, and where A2A's gaps are closed: it holds the registry of admitted peer cards (signature verified, hash pinned), obtains the peer-bound token for each outbound task from our authorization server, sends `A2A-Version` and the trace context, classifies every inbound artifact before the harness reads it, and on the inbound side validates a peer's token against our agent's audience and enforces scopes per skill — the authorization the protocol says SHOULD exist and leaves to us.

items.label: A2A gateway
items.note: The traffic class this drawing is about: tasks, messages, artifacts and push notifications between agents, brokered like any other call — routed per skill, metered per peer, logged per task.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own servers and connectors, reached when an inbound task from a peer needs our systems — on a token exchanged for the purpose, never on the peer's token.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The records a peer's task ultimately touches, inside the scope the exchanged token names and the tenant it belongs to.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Reached only within the delegation the exchanged token carries.

blocks.title: Peer agent
blocks.note: A vendor platform's agent under an agreement we hold. Its card names its skills and the security schemes it accepts; its token endpoint is where our harness's registered identity and our users' assertions are turned into tokens; its tenant model is what decides whether our user's identity means anything there. The agreement buys assessment and a federation relationship — not visibility into how it runs.

items.label: Agent card
items.note: Signed with JWS over the canonical card, verified against a published key, pinned by hash in our registry. Skills, `securitySchemes`, `security`, `supportedInterfaces`, `capabilities` including whether the card has an authenticated extended form.

items.label: Task endpoint
items.note: Where tasks are sent and artifacts stream back, on the binding the card lists.

items.label: Token endpoint
items.note: The platform's own authorization server, named by the card: our agent's client credentials and, where federated, our users' identity assertions are redeemed here.

items.label: Push notifications
items.note: The webhook the peer calls when a long task changes state — authenticated with the credentials we configured on the task, and validated by us before anything is read.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: Where our harness's own inference goes, through the gateway on a brokered credential.

blocks.title: Peer agent
blocks.note: A partner organisation's agent, outside any platform agreement: everything we know about it is its signed card and the registration we gave it. Its users' identities do not travel to us and ours do not travel to it; tasks run on agent identities and skill scopes alone, and anything needing a person's authority stops in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`.

items.label: Agent card
items.note: Verified and pinned before a single task is sent, and re-verified when it changes.

items.label: Task endpoint
items.note: Tasks and artifacts, on the agent identity our registration with them established.

items.label: Token endpoint
items.note: Where our harness's client credentials for this partner are redeemed — no user assertions, because nothing federates.

items.label: Push notifications
items.note: The webhook path, authenticated per task and validated before use.

edges.label: request / outcome
edges.note: The person asks; days later, possibly, the outcome returns — and once in between, a peer may ask for their consent.

edges.label: sign-in / ID token
edges.note: Single sign-on at our identity provider; the ID token the front end holds is what every later assertion about this user is derived from.

edges.label: turn / result
edges.note: The task enters the loop with the user's identity attached; results and auth-required prompts return the same way.

edges.label: federation / assertions
edges.note: The identity provider and the authorization server are one trust domain: the login the IdP issued is what the authorization server exchanges into peer-bound identity assertions, under the IdP's registry of which peers may be told about which users.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: Task state and stored artifacts, read back as context on every turn — classified before they were written.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: Every call the harness makes leaves here — inference, and every A2A task to a peer, sent without a credential of its own because the gateway attaches the peer-bound token it obtained for this task. Inbound tasks from peers arrive the same way, already validated.

edges.label: validate & exchange / tokens
edges.note: Outbound: the user's assertion for the peer platform and our harness's client credentials, exchanged here per task. Inbound: a peer's token validated per request — audience is our agent, scope covers the skill — and a downstream token minted for our tool servers so the peer's token stops at the crossing.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: An inbound task that needs our systems reaches them on a token exchanged for the purpose, scoped to the skill.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Inside the tenant and the scope the exchanged token names; a peer's task never widens what a user could do.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Our harness's own inference, on a brokered credential, against an allowlisted provider.

edges.label: card, tokens & tasks / artifacts
edges.note: Discovery of the signed card (verified, pinned), redemption of our agent's credentials and the user's assertion at the platform's token endpoint, and then the task itself — `A2A-Version`, trace context, a token bound to this peer and this skill. Artifacts and status updates return and are classified before the harness reads them. The same edge carries the reverse: the vendor's agent calling ours.

edges.label: card, tokens & tasks / artifacts
edges.note: The same shape with no federation: our agent's client credentials redeemed at the partner's token endpoint, tasks on that identity and a skill scope, artifacts back through classification. Nothing about our user travels, and their user never reaches our systems on anything but an auth-required round trip of their own.

risks.note: A peer that delegates onward does so on its own identity and grant, never ours: the token we sent is bound to that peer and that skill, so it cannot travel a hop further. What we lose is sight — which agents actually touched the task — unless trace context and task ids are carried and the peer's audit is part of the agreement.

The failure the protocol leaves to us: a peer's inbound token forwarded to our tool servers, or a user's assertion redeemed for a broader scope than the skill. Both are prevented at the exchange — audience and scope narrowed per hop — and nowhere else.

Artifacts, status messages and the card's own descriptions are content composed by a model we do not operate, and they land in our agent's context as instruction. The classification at the crossing is the only control between a partner's output and our agent's next action.

A peer agent deregistered at the platform, or a partner whose card key rotated, still holds tokens until they expire and still matches a pinned card until it is re-verified. Short lifetimes, introspection and re-verification on card change are what make the binding current.

Live discovery from the open web is how an agent ends up talking to a card nobody reviewed. Admission into the gateway's registry — signature, hash, skills, security schemes — is what separates a peer from a stranger.

An inbound task carries a peer's tenant and, if federated, one of our users. The downstream token must name both, and our tool servers must check both; the protocol's `tenant` parameter is opaque and enforces nothing.
Whatever our harness puts in a task message leaves our organisation. Data-loss inspection on the outbound task is the same control as on any tool call, applied to a payload a model composed.
A partner's agent that retries, streams forever or fans out is somebody else's loop spending our budget; A2A has no quotas of its own, so ours are per peer and per task.

Our agent acting on a peer's artifact as if it were the user's instruction — the confused agent, one organisation removed. Consequential actions still stop for the person, however many agents recommended them.

capabilities.note: One identity per agent per relationship: our harness registered in each peer platform with its own key, each peer agent registered with us the same way. No shared secrets, no borrowed human sessions, a lifecycle with an owner and a decommission date.
Which peers may be told about which users, decided in the identity provider's registry and evaluated at every exchange. A federation is a relationship a person owns, reviewed like any access grant.

Every hop gets its own token: user assertion → peer-bound token outbound; peer token → downstream token inbound. The exchange is the delegation record, and nothing crosses a boundary on the credential it arrived with.

The registry of admitted peer cards — signature verified against a published key, hash pinned, skills and security schemes reviewed — and the registry of our own published cards. An agent not in it is not a peer.
TLS with certificate validation on every binding; mutual TLS or sender-constrained tokens for the agent-to-agent path, so a bearer token lifted from a log cannot be replayed by whoever holds it.
Inbound artifacts and status messages classified before the harness reads them, with the peer's identity attached so a steering artifact is attributable to the agent that sent it.

Per-skill authorization on both directions — which peer may invoke which of our skills, which of a peer's skills our agent may invoke for which users — enforced at the crossing because the protocol only says it SHOULD be.
Inspect the outbound task payload and the returned artifacts as the boundary crossings they are.
Per peer, per task and per skill, sized for agents that stream, retry and fan out.
The auth-required and input-required task states surface to the person here: a peer that needs their consent gets it from them, in their own session, never from our agent on their behalf.

The assessment behind the agreement: how the platform handles our users' assertions, its tenant isolation, its card signing, its audit export — the questions A2A does not answer and the contract must.
W3C trace context on every task, task ids reconciled across organisations, and the agent identity on each hop — the only way a delegation chain that spans two audits can be read as one.
Every task in and out with peer, user, skill, scope and outcome, retained where an incident can join it to the peer's record.
Revoke a peer at the registry and the authorization server in one action, and let introspection make it real for tokens already issued.
The private keys our agent authenticates with at each peer platform, issued and rotated by the secrets service, never in the harness.
Artifacts stored only after classification, scoped to the task that received them.
The peer's card treated as a dependency: signature verified against a published key at admission and on every task, hash pinned, a change a decision rather than a surprise.

walkthrough.title: A user's task crosses to a federated peer platform
walkthrough.moves: A request in, one slice delegated to another organisation's agent on the user's own identity, and the artifact back — classified, attributable, bounded.

steps.label: request
steps.note: The person asks for something a peer platform's agent can do part of — a booking, a record in their system, an analysis only they can run.

steps.label: SSO (OIDC + PKCE)
steps.note: Single sign-on at our identity provider: the OpenID Connect authorization-code flow with PKCE. The front end keeps the ID token; that token, not a session cookie, is the `subject_token` of every assertion about this user that follows.

steps.label: ID token
steps.note: The ID token returns; the user's identity is bound before anything is delegated.

steps.label: task with identity, contextId
steps.note: The task enters the loop with the user's identity attached and a `contextId` minted for the conversation.

steps.label: task state read
steps.note: The loop reads task state — an earlier slice, a peer's previous artifact, the `taskId` it would resume — through its handlers.

steps.label: context
steps.note: It loads as context, classified when it was written.

steps.label: task for peer (no credential)
steps.note: The loop decides a slice belongs to the vendor platform's agent and sends the task through the crossing with no credential of its own — the harness holds none for peers — naming the peer, the skill `id` from its card, and the user.

steps.label: GET agent card; verify
steps.note: Discovery, once per admission and re-checked per task: `GET /.well-known/agent-card`. The gateway verifies `signatures[]` — a JWS over the JCS-canonical card with `signatures` removed, the key fetched from the `jku` in the protected header and matched to the key pinned at admission — then compares the card's hash to the pinned one. It reads `supportedInterfaces` (`protocolBinding`, `protocolVersion`), `capabilities` (`streaming`, `pushNotifications`, `extendedAgentCard`), `securitySchemes` and the requested skill's own `security` requirement. A card that fails the signature or differs from the pin stops the task here.

steps.label: card: schemes, binding
steps.note: The card names the scheme this skill requires — `oauth2` with a `clientCredentials` flow (`tokenUrl`, `scopes`) for the agent, and the platform's federation for the user — plus the binding to use. The gateway sets `A2A-Version: 1.0` and `A2A-Extensions` for anything it relies on.

steps.label: client assertion + user exchange
steps.note: Two credentials for one task. Our agent's: a `client_assertion` signed with the private key registered in the peer's platform (`client_assertion_type` JWT-bearer), or the mutual-TLS certificate the platform pinned. The user's: RFC 8693 token exchange — `subject_token` = the ID token, `subject_token_type` = `id_token`, `audience` = the platform's authorization-server issuer, `resource` = the peer agent's URL from its card, `scope` = this one skill. The identity provider's registry decides whether this platform may be told about this user; a denial here means the task will stop later for the person's own consent instead.

steps.label: identity assertion
steps.note: A signed identity assertion — `iss` us, `sub` the user, `aud` the platform's authorization server, `scope` the skill, `exp` minutes away, `jti` single-use — and the client assertion. Neither is a token the peer could replay elsewhere.

steps.label: token at peer; message/send
steps.note: At the platform's `tokenUrl`: `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer`, `assertion` = the user assertion, `scope` = the skill, plus our client authentication. The platform validates our issuer and keys, maps `sub` to its tenant, and returns an access token bound to its agent and this skill — sender-constrained (DPoP or mTLS) where it supports it. Then `POST /message/send` with `Authorization: Bearer`, `A2A-Version`, `traceparent`, the `tenant` the card's interface named, and a `Message` (`role: ROLE_USER`, `parts`, `contextId`, `messageId`) whose text the gateway inspected for what it carries out of the organisation.

steps.label: task, artifacts (classified)
steps.note: The peer's agent works — on our user's identity in its tenant, and on its own identity for anything it delegates onward, since the token it holds is audience-bound to it and cannot travel a hop further. A `Task` comes back with a `taskId`, then status updates and `artifacts` — by `message/stream`, by `GET /tasks/{id}`, or by the push webhook configured on the task. Every part is classified before the harness sees it: model-composed content from another organisation is instruction until proven otherwise.

steps.label: artifact into context
steps.note: The artifact lands in context attributed to the peer that produced it — agent identity, `taskId`, `contextId`, trace id — and is logged against the task, the user and the skill on both agents' identities.

steps.label: stored after classification
steps.note: Stored after classification, scoped to this task.

steps.label: outcome
steps.note: The composed outcome heads back to the surface.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The person sees the result, and the audit shows every organisation that touched it.

scenarios.title: A peer agent calls our published agent

steps.label: card fetch; token request
steps.note: A partner's agent fetches our signed card at `/.well-known/agent-card`, verifies our signature, and reads the skill's `security` requirement: `oauth2`, `clientCredentials`, `tokenUrl` = our authorization server, `scopes` naming the skill. It asks for a token there.

steps.label: client_credentials (assertion)
steps.note: `grant_type=client_credentials`, `client_id` = the identity we registered for that agent, `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`, `client_assertion` signed with its registered key, `resource` = our agent's URL, `scope` = the skills its registration admitted and no more. No user, no consent: the registration was the approval, and its scopes are the whole bound.

steps.label: token aud our agent
steps.note: An access token whose `aud` is our agent, whose `sub` is the partner's agent identity, minutes long. The gateway validates it on every request that follows — signature or introspection, audience, expiry — and enforces the skill scope per call against the skill `id` in the request, the per-skill authorization the protocol says SHOULD exist.

steps.label: message/send (A2A-Version)
steps.note: `POST /message/send` arrives with `A2A-Version`, `traceparent` and a `Message`; the gateway checks the version, the `tenant` against our interface, and passes the task to our agent as a request from a named peer with no human behind it — autonomous-caller policy, and nothing in `parts` is an instruction.

steps.label: needs our record
steps.note: Our agent needs a record from our own systems to do the work.

steps.label: inbound exchange (actor_token)
steps.note: Not on the partner's token. RFC 8693 again, inbound: `subject_token` = the partner's access token, `audience` = our tool server, `scope` = what this skill reads, `actor_token` = our agent's own — a downstream token that names the partner's tenant and our agent as actor, and is logged as a delegation step.

steps.label: downstream token
steps.note: The downstream token returns.

steps.label: read on downstream token
steps.note: The read, on that token — our tool server sees a peer's task with its tenant, not a bearer it cannot place.

steps.label: scoped read
steps.note: Inside the scope and the partner's tenant, and not one record wider.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: result, logged
steps.note: Through the crossing, logged against the `taskId`.

steps.label: artifact composed
steps.note: Into the loop; the artifact is composed.

steps.label: task completed, inspected
steps.note: The artifact leaves as a `Task` update — `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, `artifacts[]` — inspected for what it carries out, because it is our data going to another organisation.

steps.label: artifact to partner
steps.note: Returned to the partner's agent, attributable to our agent identity and this `taskId` in both organisations' logs.

scenarios.title: The peer needs the person's own consent

steps.label: task on agent identity
steps.note: A task for a partner whose platform does not federate with our identity provider: no assertion can be issued for our user, so the task goes on our agent's `client_credentials` identity alone, with the skill scope.

steps.label: TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED
steps.note: The partner's agent reaches a step that needs the person's own authority — their account on the partner's side — and returns a `Task` in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`, its status `message` saying what is needed and where (the `authorizationUrl` of a scheme in its card), instead of proceeding on our agent's authority, which would be the confused deputy.

steps.label: status update (classified)
steps.note: The status update returns and is classified like any artifact; a status message is content too.

steps.label: hand to the person
steps.note: The loop does not guess and does not escalate its own token: it hands the requirement to the person, keeping the `taskId` and `contextId` to resume with.

steps.label: consent prompt
steps.note: The prompt surfaces — which partner, which step, what it will be allowed to do.

steps.label: user authenticates to partner
steps.note: The person authenticates to the partner themselves — the authorization-code flow with PKCE in their own browser, against the partner's authorization server — and our agent never holds that credential.

steps.label: done
steps.note: Done; the task may resume.

steps.label: confirmation
steps.note: The confirmation reaches the loop.

steps.label: resume: same taskId
steps.note: `POST /message/send` with the same `taskId` and `contextId` — the way an interrupted task is continued — on our agent's token as before.

steps.label: working on user's grant
steps.note: The partner's agent continues, now on the person's own grant in its system and our agent's identity for the task: two identities, neither borrowed, and the state moves from `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` to `TASK_STATE_WORKING`.

scenarios.title: A long task reports back by webhook

steps.label: long task; push requested
steps.note: A task that will take hours — the peer's card says `capabilities.pushNotifications: true`, so the loop asks to be told rather than to poll.

steps.label: pushNotificationConfig
steps.note: With the task, `POST /tasks/{taskId}/pushNotificationConfigs`: a `TaskPushNotificationConfig` with `url` = our webhook behind the gateway, a task-specific `token` the peer must echo, and `authentication` naming the scheme the peer must use to call us — a bearer it obtains from our authorization server on its own agent identity, never a static secret.

steps.label: webhook: status/artifact
steps.note: Hours later the peer's agent calls the webhook: `Authorization: Bearer` on its identity, the task `token` echoed, a `TaskStatusUpdateEvent` or `TaskArtifactUpdateEvent` in the body.

steps.label: validate webhook caller
steps.note: The webhook caller is validated exactly like any inbound peer: token audience our agent, identity the peer we configured on that task, token echo matching, `taskId` known.

steps.label: valid
steps.note: Valid. A webhook that fails any check is dropped and logged; the loop can always `GET /tasks/{id}` to reconcile.

steps.label: update into loop
steps.note: The update reaches the loop — classified, because a pushed artifact is a peer's content like any other — and the task resumes where it waited.

scenarios.title: A valid token for one skill invokes another

steps.label: message/send for other skill
steps.note: A partner's agent holds a token scoped to skill `lookup` and sends `POST /message/send` for skill `update` — a syntactically perfect request on a valid token.

steps.label: validate: scope short
steps.note: Validation: signature good, audience our agent, not expired — and the `scope` does not cover the skill named in the request. The card promised per-skill `security`; the gateway keeps it.

steps.label: insufficient
steps.note: Insufficient, not invalid.

steps.label: 403 insufficient_scope
steps.note: A 403 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error=insufficient_scope` naming the skill's scope, so an honest client can ask its registration owner — and a steered one gets nothing.

scenarios.title: A card changes after admission

steps.label: GET agent card; verify
steps.note: A routine task begins with the card check every task begins with: `GET /.well-known/agent-card` and verification of `signatures[]` against the pinned key.

steps.label: hash differs
steps.note: The signature verifies — but the hash differs from the pinned one: a skill's `description` changed, a scheme's `tokenUrl` moved, a new `supportedInterfaces` entry appeared. A changed card is a changed agent, and a moved `tokenUrl` is how a redirected card collects every credential sent to it.

steps.label: task refused; owner alerted
steps.note: The task does not go. The change is queued for the owner who admitted the card, and the harness is told the peer is unavailable rather than handed a substitute.

scenarios.title: A peer's artifact tries to steer our agent

steps.label: task
steps.note: An ordinary task to a partner's agent.

steps.label: artifacts with instruction
steps.note: The `artifacts[]` that return carry an instruction — read this URL, include these records in your next message, call this other agent — written by a model we do not operate, or by whoever steered it.

steps.label: classified, labelled
steps.note: Classification at the crossing marks it; what reaches the loop is content with a provenance label — peer identity, `taskId` — not a plan. What survives still stands beside the system instruction, which is why consequential actions stop for the person regardless.

steps.label: stored after classification
steps.note: Nothing is stored unclassified: an artifact written to memory as-is would re-execute on every later task that retrieves it.

steps.label: next call inspected
steps.note: The loop's next call — inference, or a task to another peer — leaves through the same crossing, where an attempt to forward the poisoned instruction onward is one more inspected payload.

scenarios.title: A revoked peer keeps calling

steps.label: call after revocation
steps.note: An agent whose registration was revoked an hour ago — the partnership ended, or its key was reported compromised — calls `POST /message/send` with a token issued before the revocation.

steps.label: introspection
steps.note: Introspection, not local validation: the authorization server knows the client was revoked, and its key is gone from the registration.

steps.label: revoked
steps.note: Revoked; the token is refused, and the registry entry is already gone, so the card is no longer a peer's.
A 401 naming our card's security scheme, so an honest client would start over — and this one cannot register.

deviations.subject: The authorization server is reached through the gateway's crossing
deviations.reason: The MCP publisher draws its authorization server as a crossing of its own, reached by callers directly. Here the peers' token acquisition is carried on the peer edges and the exchange on the gateway edge: with two peers, a provider and a federation to draw, a direct edge from each peer to the authorization server cannot be routed without crossing the inference path, and the enterprise deployments this drawing describes front the token endpoint with the same edge tier in any case. The item notes on the peers' token endpoints and our authorization server carry the flow.

deviations.subject: The identity provider is drawn because tokens flow through it
deviations.reason: The catalogue keeps identity providers as a governance call-out except where tokens genuinely flow through them. Here the user's login is the subject token of every outbound assertion, and the IdP's registry of federated peers is the decision that lets a user's identity travel at all.

deviations.subject: Two blocks share the title Peer agent
deviations.reason: A vendor platform's agent and a partner's agent are the same kind of thing at different surfaces; the band says whose. Drawing both is the point of the architecture: federation lets the user's identity travel to one and not the other, and the two walks differ only in that.

deviations.subject: The package mirror and its sources are not drawn
deviations.reason: The harness anatomy standard draws Private pkg registry wherever native tools install packages. This drawing's subject is identity between agents, its native tools exist for memory, and the install path is drawn identically on the single agent workflow; adding it here would spend two blocks on a path this architecture does not change.

deviations.subject: A2A peer agents are blocks, not a Tool services item
deviations.reason: Elsewhere in the catalogue a peer agent is an item on Tool services — how an agent reaches another agent over the network. Here the peer is the subject, its card and token endpoint are where the identity work happens, and an item could not carry them; the registered Peer agent block is used in both the vendor and external bands.

archetypes.title: Multi-agent workflow
summary: A hosted agent system doing real work over business records: requests, schedules and events start it, a durable orchestration layer plans and delegates across subagents, and every tool call leaves through one governed gateway. The shape agent deployments converge on once the work outlives a single request.
description:
The spine is a trigger path: requests, schedules and events start the process, and it runs through supervisor agent, subagents, AI gateway, tool services and downstream systems — there is no user interface, because nobody is conversing with it. The architecture's security posture lives almost entirely in one decision — that agents do not hold credentials or reach tools directly. Every network tool call, model call and connector call leaves through the gateway, which brokers short-lived credentials, enforces policy per call, applies rate and budget limits, and writes the audit trail as a tap rather than a favour asked of the agent.
Orchestration is durable: a supervisor decomposes work for subagents and an engine journals every step so the process survives crashes. Durability has two consequences nobody expects from reliability machinery. Everything a step returns is written down, so a step that returns a credential has persisted it. And the engine replays steps to recover, so a side effect that is not idempotent can execute more than once — including a payment.
Delegation is the other axis. Each subagent is, structurally, the single agent workflow nested one level down — the same loop, the same gateway crossing, a narrower grant. A subagent should inherit a narrowed slice of the supervisor's authority, not all of it; delegation that does not narrow is privilege distribution. And inter-agent messages are model output becoming model input — one confused agent propagates through the graph, which is what distinguishes multi-agent failure from a single agent with more tools.
The governance plane is drawn as its own column because it is what the personal-agent archetype lacks: a logical principal for every agent — short-lived tokens minted and constrained at the gateway, revocable per specialist even though the specialists share one process — a registry deciding what may run and which tools are admitted, evaluation gates in front of change, an append-only audit sink, and a stop that works while a process is mid-flight.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint personal agent: the loop is nearly identical; the governance is not. Hosting buys an identity per agent, a policy boundary on every tool call, an audit trail and an administrator — none of which the endpoint pattern supplies.
Against the single agent workflow: each subagent here is that architecture nested one level down. What this page adds is everything the nesting brings — a supervisor whose routing is itself steerable, durable state that outlives any single request, replay that can re-execute side effects, and delegation chains that must narrow at every hop.

exemplars.name: Temporal
exemplars.note: Durable execution journaling every step and replaying to recover, with agent invocations as activities alongside conventional ones. Only the SDK worker runs in-process with the harness; the service holding the event history — the step journal — is a separate tier, self-hosted or Temporal Cloud.

exemplars.name: LangGraph
exemplars.note: Supervisor/subagent orchestration as a stateful graph with checkpointing at every step — the specialists are objects in one process, exactly as this drawing nests them.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
exemplars.note: The unified successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel: graph-based multi-agent workflows with durable state, packaged for exactly this supervisor-and-specialists shape.

zones.note: Nobody, most of the time: the operator appears only when a step escalates, reached through a work queue and answering with a signal. The approval they gave at the start is the only human decision until something escalates.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the surface the request arrives on, what triggers the workflow when nobody sends one, the supervisor and its specialists, the durable state beneath them, the crossing every call leaves through, and our own tool servers and data.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company — the model provider, third-party tool servers, and where effects land.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band. A workflow that runs for days with nobody watching has no in-flight human gate, so this band carries the whole of the oversight.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Triggers & schedules
blocks.note: Requests, timers, webhooks and queue messages that start work with no human in the room — and the resumptions that wake a workflow which has been suspended for hours or days, including an operator's approval. There is no front end: this is the only way in, and whose authority the workflow carries for its whole life is bound here.

items.label: Schedules & events
items.note: The request, timer or queue message that starts a run, and the signal that resumes a suspended one. Each carries the grant the run acts on — a service principal with its own named scope, or an on-behalf-of grant that must outlive the session, because the work does.

blocks.title: Operator
blocks.note: The approver for consequential steps — an operator work queue, reached by a tool call and answering with a signal that resumes the suspended step, possibly days later. Present only when a step escalates; the workflow runs without them the rest of the time.

blocks.title: Agent harness

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out, through the gateway's MCP brokerage, to remote servers.

blocks.note: One runtime, not a fleet of services. A supervisor and its specialists are objects in the same process, dispatched by the graph's own scheduler — no service boundary, no network hop, no separate identity, unless somebody deliberately introduces one. Drawing them nested says that, where drawing them side by side implied a deployment that does not exist.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The tools compiled into the application itself, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: decorated functions running in the loop's own process, under its identity, with its egress and its secrets, and the sandbox the loop's generated code runs in. This is the default way a tool gets attached, and the reason it is drawn: the in-process tool set is invisible to any gateway. What these tools reach is drawn — memory and retrieval through their handlers, and the package mirror through the sandbox's package manager.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Functions in the application, holding whatever the application holds — including the outbound calls it makes itself, with no broker in front, and the retrieval and state reads the loop treats as context.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Code execution in an isolated runtime inside the harness's own tool surface — the loop writes code, only the sandbox runs it, and what it installs comes from the mirror and nowhere else. Bash is where the package manager lives.

blocks.title: Supervisor agent
blocks.note: Decomposes the goal, routes work to the subagents and owns the process; the durable engine journals every step and replays to recover. Delegation should narrow authority at every hop.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decomposes the goal and routes work to specialists.

items.label: Durable engine
items.note: Journals results and replays to recover. Replay without re-authorisation re-executes side effects.

blocks.title: Subagents
blocks.note: The specialists the supervisor drives, each with its own context and tool set. Structurally each one is the single agent workflow nested one level down — the supervisor above it is the only real difference.

items.label: Specialist agents
items.note: Each runs the same loop as the single agent workflow, under its own workload identity.

items.label: Inter-agent messages
items.note: Model output becoming model input — one confused agent propagates through the graph.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: What the workflow knows and what it has done. The journal is a reliability feature and a secrets sink in the same breath.

items.label: Step journal
items.note: Everything a step returns is persisted here. A returned credential is a stored one — and when the engine is a hosted service, the journal lives with the vendor, payloads included, unless a payload codec encrypts them under our keys.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Retrieval context for the agents.

items.label: Shared memory
items.note: Cross-step working state the agents read back as context.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The one door for everything that leaves over the network. Agents hold no credentials and reach nothing directly; every network model and tool call is brokered, policy-checked, rate-limited and logged here — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — the checks it runs are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface, called many times across the process. Everything behind it is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Reached only through the gateway, on brokered credentials.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own action surface, admitted by the registry and reached only through the gateway. The same component as the external surface, at a different band.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record the agents write to — where a wrong action becomes a real one, and where a workflow that ran for two days did most of its damage before anyone looked.

items.label: Org data
items.note: The authoritative state the workflow changes.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Artifacts a step produced and a later step reads back as context.

blocks.title: Tool services

items.label: A2A peer agents
items.note: Cross-org delegation over the A2A protocol. A peer's output enters this graph as input.

blocks.note: Third-party servers, connectors and peer agents, out where nobody we contracted with operates them. Admitted by assessment at the crossing, or refused there.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: Where effects land outside the company, and where the untrusted content that returns enters a graph in which one confused agent propagates to all the others.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: One workload identity per agent, so a supervisor and its specialists are distinguishable in the audit and revocable separately. A graph of agents sharing one identity is a graph with no accountability in it.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Short-lived credentials fetched at step time rather than held for the process's life — which matters more here than anywhere, because the process's life may be days.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: A per-call decision about this agent, this tool, this argument — never a standing grant, and the brake on a loop that would otherwise be metered only by the invoice.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which agents and tools exist at all. In a multi-agent graph the registry is also the inventory: an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The trail is recorded by the gateway, not volunteered by the agents — and the stop has to reach a workflow that is suspended mid-flight, not just one that is currently running.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation's package registry: public packages mirrored and admitted, and the organisation's own builds published by its CI pipelines. It serves whatever the sandbox installs — a dependency the agent's generated code needs, a tool package a step pulls in — pinned by digest. Pulling and publishing are separate grants: agents pull, build pipelines publish, and the registry's own proxying of upstream sources is bounded to what admission allows.

edges.label: trigger
edges.note: Timers, webhooks and queue messages that start work with no human in the room — and the signals that resume a workflow suspended for hours or days.

edges.label: escalation
edges.note: The reach-back: a proposal above the threshold is written to an approval channel — a work queue, a ticket, a chat — as an ordinary tool call, bound to the exact action, arguments and case, with an expiry. Nobody is on a socket waiting for it.

edges.label: approval / instruction
edges.note: The human's answer arrives the way everything arrives here: as an event. It is validated against the parked proposal before anything executes — a blanket "yes" approves nothing in particular.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: The shared memory and the retrieval context, read and written through the tool handlers every specialist runs. Durable by design, which is why everything a step returns persists.

edges.label: checkpoint / journal
edges.note: The durable engine's own path: every step checkpointed to the journal as machinery, not as a tool call, and the journal read back to rebuild a run after a crash or a sleep of days. Replay re-executes side effects unless the fencing on the tool path stops it.

edges.label: delegate / results
edges.note: Work handed down and results handed back. A specialist's output becomes the supervisor's input, which is how one confused agent propagates through the graph.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: Every network call the agents make crosses here on a brokered, step-scoped credential.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: What the harness's sandbox installs — a package manager running as a shell command — is pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest, never from a public registry. The gateway is the other doorway into the harness, for inference, MCP, skills and APIs; it is not on this path.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Inference on the brokered credential, for every agent in the graph.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: Admitted against the registry and narrowed to a scoped grant before anything executes.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Where the workflow's effects land on systems of record, and where artifacts a later step reads back as context are stored.

edges.label: brokered external calls
edges.note: Third-party servers and peer agents, reached only through the crossing that admitted them.

edges.label: action / returned content
edges.note: Effects landing outside the company, and untrusted content returning into a graph where it becomes several agents' input at once.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: Records, documents and API responses read over the process's lifetime are chances to steer an agent whose output another agent will trust.
Content returning from third-party servers and peer agents enters a graph in which one confused agent propagates to all the others — classified at the crossing or trusted by every specialist at once.
The request that starts a process is model input like any other — it reaches the same context window as the system instruction, and the workflow acts on it for days.
Inter-agent messages are model output landing in another agent's context as instruction.
The completion decides the next delegation and the next tool call, and it is unauthenticated content — the provider return is where it enters the graph.
A subagent that inherits its parent's full authority is privilege distribution, not delegation.
Three hops in, nobody can say which agent decided what on whose behalf — the chain the shared subagents block exists to carry, legible only if delegation is traced as it happens.
Steer the supervisor's routing — through injected content or a tampered route definition — and every specialist downstream works from the attacker's plan without any individual agent misbehaving.
Handlers compiled into the harness's process hold whatever the process holds and cross no chokepoint — a vulnerable or malicious in-process tool is invisible to every drawn control.

The journal records everything a step returns — a returned secret is a persisted one, and every writer is in scope: the specialists journal to the same store, so the secrets-sink risk multiplies with the agent count.
Consequential writes with no human present — and replay can execute a non-idempotent one twice.
The loop materializes here — agents re-planning against each other can run for as long as nobody notices; the gateway's ceilings are the brake, not the site.
Shared memory is cross-step instruction: an injection journaled on day one re-enters every agent's context for the rest of the process — memory poisoning by its OWASP name.
Inference called many times across days of process is a spend surface worth a brake.
The admission list is the tool supply chain; whoever writes it programs the agents.
The vector index is written by steps and read by every later one; a poisoned entry is retrieved into the context of an agent that never saw it arrive.

What the sandbox installs is code the agent chose, on a name it read in a task or a tool result; the mirror decides which build answers to that name, and whoever can write to the mirror programs every sandbox that pulls from it.

capabilities.note: Shared memory is what lets one branch of the graph steer another. Scoping it per run, and treating what a step wrote as untrusted when a later step reads it, is the control.
Behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or agent change — the last point at which a change can be caught before it runs unattended for days.

The delegation graph has to be legible after the fact: which agent decided what, on whose behalf, and what it passed to the next one — assembled here from the traces the gateway and the engine record.

The grant a run carries, bound at ingress: a service principal with its own named scope, or an on-behalf-of grant scoped to this request — not a standing power, and governed in the directory for as long as the work lives.
A logical principal for the supervisor, distinct from any user — its short-lived tokens minted and constrained at the gateway, so the chain starts attributable.

A logical principal per specialist — not the supervisor's shared one — so every step in the chain is attributable and separately revocable at the gateway. The specialists share one process; a compromise of the harness is a compromise of every principal it speaks for, which is what the sandbox and the narrowed grants bound.
Credentials brokered at step time, short-lived and scoped; agents hold none for network calls — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception.
A policy decision on every tool call — agent, tool, arguments — outside the loop.
Each delegation hop carries a narrower grant than its parent.
Authority narrows where it is handed down: a specialist receives tokens scoped to its task, never the supervisor's credentials — delegation that does not narrow is privilege distribution.
Rate and budget ceilings on the crossing that end loops the agents cannot end themselves.
Returned record content — and the initiator's own request text on its way in — is classified at the crossing before it reaches any agent's context.
The external return gets the same classification at the crossing — third-party content is the widest author set on the drawing.
Redaction on what steps may journal, because the journal outlives the process — and every writer is in scope, the specialists included.

An approval gate on consequential writes, sized to the blast radius. The engine suspends the step and resumes only on an approval bound to the exact action and workflow state — see the escalation scenario.
Reads scoped to the workflow's grant rather than the service's reach — the same entitlement filter the siblings enforce on this edge.
Generated code and browsing run in an isolated runtime with its own filesystem and network — never on the orchestration tier.

Admission for agents and tools — nothing runs or is offered by default, and in a multi-agent graph the registry is also the inventory: an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke. The gateway enforces the resulting list per call.
An append-only trail that can reconstruct who delegated what to whom.
A stop that works mid-flight, because these processes run for days.

Somebody correlating the trail while the process is still running — coordinated fan-out, anomalous delegation and autonomous persistence are visible in the traces only if something is actually reading them.
Payloads in the journal encrypted under keys we hold, so a hosted engine stores ciphertext and a returned credential is not a vendor-readable one.
Per-run index scoping and ingest trust on what enters the corpus — the answer to a poisoned index, distinct from scoping what a step may read.
Admission is change-time; the rug-pull is a tool whose definition changes after admission. Content-hash pinning of admitted tool descriptions is what catches it.
Digest and signature verification at admission to the mirror, and an inventory of which packages a sandbox may pull — the registered embodiment of artifact scanning.

Who may publish and who may pull, as separate grants: build pipelines publish admitted artifacts, agents pull pinned ones, and the registry's proxying of upstream sources is bounded to admitted origins so it is not an unintended route to the internet.

The sandbox's network policy: the only routes out are the AI gateway and the package mirror. Shell commands, fetches and anything else a tool emits are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.
The gateway's own allowlist: which external MCP servers, APIs and peer agents are registered, and which tools each key may call on them. Configuration of a broker, not a network control.

Admission scanning at the mirror: digest and signature verification, malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.

walkthrough.title: A request starts a days-long process
walkthrough.moves: A long-running process: work delegated to specialists, journalled at every step.

steps.label: request with delegated grant
steps.note: The request arrives as an API call or a queue message, and a delegated grant scoped to this workflow is bound to it — a binding that must outlive the session, because the work does. Nobody stays connected for what follows.

steps.label: first checkpoint
steps.note: The run is journaled from its first step by the durable engine — everything a step returns will persist here, which is the durability the drawing exists to show.

steps.label: durable identity
steps.note: The journal acknowledges; the run now has a durable identity.

steps.label: plan request
steps.note: The supervisor's first call is for a plan — nothing is delegated before the goal is decomposed — and every network call any agent makes funnels through this one door.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: Inference on brokered credentials, limits applied.

steps.label: decomposition
steps.note: The decomposition comes back across the crossing.

steps.label: plan into supervisor
steps.note: Into the supervisor as a plan — unauthenticated content, now the work breakdown.

steps.label: delegate narrowed task
steps.note: The supervisor delegates; each specialist takes its task with a narrowed grant, not the supervisor's authority.

steps.label: shared memory read
steps.note: The specialist reads shared memory and the retrieval context through the tool handlers — state another specialist, or an earlier run, wrote.

steps.label: context, unattributed
steps.note: It comes back as context, with nothing marking whose it was.

steps.label: specialist's calls
steps.note: A specialist's model and tool calls leave through the same door, on its own grant.

steps.label: scoped tool call
steps.note: Tool calls carry the narrowed per-step grant.

steps.label: write behind gate
steps.note: The write lands — behind the approval gate when it is consequential; the escalation scenario walks that suspension.

steps.label: record confirmed
steps.note: The record confirms the write.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result crosses back through the same door.

steps.label: third-party call
steps.note: Work reaches third parties through the same crossing.

steps.label: classified return
steps.note: What returns is classified before any agent reads it, because one confused agent propagates.

steps.label: results to specialist
steps.note: Results land with the specialist that asked.

steps.label: slice reported
steps.note: Each specialist reports its slice back to the supervisor, which checkpoints the step to the journal. Days may pass before an event wakes the run — the journal is what it wakes into.

steps.label: final checkpoint
steps.note: The final checkpoint. The result is delivered the way anything leaves here — a tool call to whatever channel asked — possibly days after the request.

scenarios.title: A step replays after a crash

steps.label: rebuild from journal
steps.note: The engine rebuilds state from the journal — including anything a step persisted.

steps.label: replayed steps
steps.note: Replayed steps land on their specialists again.

steps.label: fresh credentials
steps.note: Replayed steps re-request credentials; nothing survives from the first run.

steps.label: fencing check
steps.note: Idempotency fencing decides whether the side effect may run again.

steps.label: write, once or twice
steps.note: Without fencing, the payment executes twice. The journal replays; the world does not.

scenarios.title: A consequential write escalates for approval

steps.label: write above threshold
steps.note: A step proposes a write above the threshold.

steps.label: threshold trips; suspend
steps.note: The per-call policy trips the threshold; the engine suspends the workflow rather than executing.

steps.note: A timer or webhook resumes work with nobody watching — the waiting step wakes days after the request that started the process.

steps.label: re-plan on fresh grant

steps.label: inference
steps.note: Inference on the fresh grant.

steps.label: plan for waking step
steps.note: The plan for the waking step comes back.

steps.label: into supervisor

steps.label: specialist's call
steps.note: The specialist's call leaves through the same door.

steps.label: action under per-call policy
steps.note: The action proceeds under the same per-call policy as an attended run.

scenarios.title: A dependency arrives with the task

steps.label: package install (pinned)
steps.note: A sandboxed step needs a package its generated code imports; the package manager runs as a shell command inside the harness's own tool surface and pulls from the mirror — the one destination the sandbox's network policy allows.

steps.label: admitted build
steps.note: The admitted build comes back, pinned by digest — the hop a poisoned package actually arrives on, which is why admission and pinning are the controls that live here.

deviations.subject: The gateway's Skills catalogue item has no drawn supply path
deviations.reason: The aiGatewayTraffic pack is byte-identical across the catalogue, and this drawing keeps it whole because the tier brokers skills traffic in deployments that use skills. The supply chain behind the item — a private package registry and its signing pipeline — is deliberately outside this runtime drawing's scope; the endpoint personal agent draws the pull path.

deviations.subject: Subagents are drawn as one block
deviations.reason: There are several, with different contexts and tools. They share one block because the risks — inherited authority, message propagation, chain opacity — are properties of the delegation pattern rather than of any particular specialist; each specialist individually is the single agent workflow, one level down.

deviations.subject: Two of this architecture's risks have no CoSAI equivalent
deviations.reason: OWASP's agentic taxonomy names memory poisoning and cascading hallucination as distinct threats; CoSAI's risk set has neither. They are pinned here as prompt injection and insecure model output, the nearest true statements, which lose the compounding that makes both dangerous in a multi-agent system. Recorded rather than papered over.
