archetypes.title: Self-hosted model inference
summary: An open-weights model served on infrastructure the organisation operates — the same inference runtime as the endpoint local model runtime, with an AI gateway in front of it and a governance plane behind it. Weights land in storage from a public hub or the organisation's own fine-tuning pipeline, and the whole model-provider role moves inside the boundary.
description:
The trade is explicit: the provider-boundary disclosure risk goes away and a supply-chain, availability and safety risk arrives — while logs, caches, storage and co-tenancy keep their own disclosure paths in-house. There is no provider applying content policy, no provider absorbing a traffic spike, and no provider patching the serving stack. Every control a managed API supplies by default is now a component this organisation runs or does without — which is why the gateway and the governance plane are the blocks that separate this architecture from the same software installed by one person on a workstation.
The supply chain is the distinctive risk. Weights are large artifacts that arrive in storage from a public hub or from the organisation's own fine-tuning pipeline, and several distribution formats execute code on load. The control is scanning and format policy in the promotion gate, before an artifact reaches the runtime — a blocking gate, not a report — and digest verification at load, so the gate cannot be bypassed by writing to storage directly.
Multi-tenancy inside the runtime has no equivalent elsewhere in this catalogue. Continuous batching mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass on shared accelerators, the KV cache holds their context, and prefix caching across tenants is a performance feature that is also a disclosure path. Whether cache entries may be shared across tenants is a serving configuration flag with data-protection consequences, and it rarely reaches a review.
Availability is a security property here in a way it is not with a managed API. Capacity is finite and expensive, admission control at the gateway is what stops one caller becoming everyone else's outage, and quotas are a control rather than a billing feature.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint local model runtime: identical software, entirely different operational position. There it was installed by one person and has no inventory entry; here it has a gateway in front, a promotion pipeline, an identity and someone on call.
Against consuming a managed model API: this architecture replaces one boundary crossing with a whole subsystem. The guardrails, abuse monitoring, capacity management and patching the provider was doing are now blocks on this diagram.

exemplars.name: vLLM
exemplars.note: The serving runtime this drawing's runtime block describes — continuous batching, paged attention, prefix caching — whose security guide documents the opt-in API key, the unauthenticated auxiliary endpoints and the trusted-network assumption the notes cite.

exemplars.name: KServe
exemplars.note: Model serving on Kubernetes with an inference-aware routing layer in front — the cluster-scheduled shape of this architecture, storage-to-runtime load path included.

exemplars.name: SGLang
exemplars.note: A second serving stack with the same co-tenancy mechanics (radix-tree prefix caching across requests), illustrating that the cache-sharing disclosure path is a property of the class, not one product.

zones.note: Everything we operate. This architecture is almost entirely one band, which is the point: the organisation took the model in-house and inherited every control the provider was applying on the way in and out.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company — the public hubs and pipelines the weights arrive from.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band. With no vendor and no human in the request path, admission of the artifact and inventory of the runtime are most of what governance can do here.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Consuming applications
blocks.note: Internal applications and agents sharing one cluster. Their isolation from each other is a property of the serving configuration, not of the network between them.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The governed front door in front of finite capacity — the same gateway block every hosted architecture in this catalogue routes through. With no provider applying content policy, the guardrail checks enforced here are a service the organisation runs itself or does without. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — the checks it runs are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

items.label: Model proxy
items.note: The one traffic class this gateway carries — inference, brokered per tenant.

blocks.title: Inference API
blocks.note: The OpenAI-compatible endpoint the serving stack publishes — the same component the local runtime draws, at a different scale. Authentication here is opt-in too: vLLM's `--api-key` is a flag, not a default, and a serving tier reachable without one is the same failure as an unauthenticated laptop, with a much larger blast radius.

items.label: Completion endpoint
items.note: The published interface every internal caller shares.

items.label: Interface binding
items.note: Which network the tier is reachable from, and the whole of the trust boundary if auth is off.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: The same runtime the endpoint architecture draws — loading weights, batching requests, serving completions — operated here as a shared service across tenants on shared accelerators. The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and its distributed control plane assumes a trusted network: job APIs and inter-node channels ship unauthenticated by design, so network isolation is a control, not a hardening step.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Where a pickle-based format turns file opening into code execution — and where the registry digest is verified.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: Open weights with no provider-side guardrail, abuse monitoring or content policy.

items.label: Continuous batching
items.note: Mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass on shared accelerators. Efficiency and co-tenancy are the same mechanism.

items.label: KV & prefix cache
items.note: Tenants' live context, held to avoid recomputing it. Sharing prefixes across tenants is a performance feature and a disclosure path in the same flag.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Versioned weight artifacts with provenance and a promotion state — expensive to reproduce, trivial to copy. Nothing serves that was not promoted, provided the load path verifies the digest.

items.label: Model files
items.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts whose format determines whether loading them is deserialization or execution.

blocks.title: Model sources
blocks.note: Where hub weights come from: a public catalogue, where publisher identity says nothing about what the artifact does on load. The organisation's own fine-tuned models do not enter here — they arrive from the model registry, inside our custody.

items.label: Open-weights catalogue
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Workload identity per calling tenant — the thing every quota, cache-isolation and attribution decision on this page keys off, issued by the platform rather than a shared key in a config map.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Format and content inspection as a blocking gate in the promotion pipeline, and the record of which artifact is actually serving. The control a managed provider would have supplied, now operated in-house.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Per-tenant ceilings on finite capacity — what stops one caller becoming everyone's outage — and the content policy no provider is applying any more.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The internal credentials this system runs on — storage pulls, registry reads, control-plane tokens — and the weights themselves treated as an asset worth protecting rather than a file on a disk.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Which versions serve where and at what configuration — including whether cross-tenant cache sharing is on — plus per-version red teaming, because a new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested.

blocks.title: Model registry
blocks.note: The fine-tuning pipeline's output, and the block the two drawings share literally: a promoted release arrives here signed by an identity the training job never held, with lineage back to its data, base and run. What it publishes needs no second gate — its signature and lineage are verified, not re-evaluated.

items.label: Signed releases
items.note: Signature and lineage are the admission evidence; withdrawal here is refusal at load everywhere.

edges.label: inference request
edges.note: The tenant on the token is what quotas and cache-isolation decisions key off. A request that arrives without one gets whatever the default tenant can do.

edges.label: brokered inference
edges.note: Every caller crosses the gateway, which is where the tenant identity, the per-tenant quota and the spend attribution live — the things the endpoint drawing has nowhere to put.

edges.label: request / completion
edges.note: Admitted requests scheduled into the batch; completions back through the guardrail checks. Output-side policy is the half most often omitted when self-hosting.

edges.label: promoted release
edges.note: A signed release lands in the store with its promotion record; the load path verifies the signature against it. This is where this drawing meets the training pipeline.

edges.label: weights in
edges.note: Artifacts arrive in storage — fetched from the hub by the ingest tooling, or published by the fine-tuning pipeline's registry. The serving runtime holds no source-fetch credentials; provenance establishes who made the artifact and nothing about what it does on load.

edges.label: load
edges.note: Only promoted artifacts load, digest-verified against the promotion record. Without that verification the gate can be bypassed by writing to storage directly.

risks.note: The endpoint's own exposure, distinct from the cache story pinned on the runtime: authentication is opt-in on this class of server, and a completion endpoint reachable without it hands every tenant's model to whatever can route to the binding.
Publisher identity is the only assurance the hub offers, and it says nothing about the artifact's behaviour.
Several weight formats execute code on load, and the loader is where the file is opened. Format policy at promotion is what keeps this leg deserialization rather than execution.
The stored artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy, which makes storage access control an asset-protection question.
A load path that skips digest verification turns the promotion gate into a suggestion.
The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and no provider is patching it on anyone's behalf.

The gateway is third-party code holding every tenant's brokered credentials — a compromised release of the gateway itself is the whole credential portfolio, a supply chain incident class with recent precedent.
Shared accelerators are a physical substrate common to every tenant, below every namespace boundary.

The sharpest risk that exists here and not on the endpoint. Continuous batching mixes several tenants' requests into one forward pass, and prefix caching makes time-to-first-token a side channel — a crafted prefix plus response timing is enough to reconstruct prompts and secrets cached from another tenant's request. Efficiency and isolation are the same settings; partition the cache by tenant, and note the risk compounds under disaggregated serving, where the cache crosses the network onto SSD and object storage.

Sustained query access is all extraction needs, and every internal caller — or whatever compromises one — has it. A proprietary fine-tune distilled out through its own completion endpoint is theft that looks like traffic; rate ceilings and anomaly review on the crossing are the answer.
Capacity is finite and there is no provider to absorb a spike. Admission control here is an availability control, not a billing feature.
With no provider applying output policy, an unguarded return leg hands raw completions to every caller.
Dynamic adapter-loading endpoints load LoRA weights at runtime by path — a second load path that skips storage, the digest and the promotion gate, and one the serving stack ships behind a flag.
Weight-update, pause and abort endpoints outside the versioned API are not covered by the API key on the common serving stacks; reachable from a tenant, they swap the model under every other tenant.

The compile and torch caches are loaded without integrity verification, in formats that can execute; a writable cache directory is a write-to-execute path the serving stack's own guide says never to share.

capabilities.note: Verify at load, not at download. For a promoted release that is the OpenSSF Model Signing signature with its Sigstore bundle — a detached signature, so nothing has to be repackaged; for a hub artifact, which mostly carries none, it is the promotion record's digest. This is the gate between the store and the loader.
The record of which artifact is actually serving — publisher, version, format and the scan that cleared it. Without it the question "what is running" has no answer.
The internal credentials the crossing brokers — storage pulls, registry reads, control-plane tokens — issued short-lived per call rather than living in the serving tier's environment.

Every request and completion recorded from the tap at the crossing every caller shares, kept privacy-consciously: the log of an inference service is itself a corpus of everything the organisation asked.
Per model version, because a new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested — and there is no provider doing it on our behalf.
Format and content scanning as a blocking gate on ingest, before any artifact can be promoted — absorbed by the promotion gate over Storage, per the recorded deviation.
Safety and adversarial evaluation per model version gates promotion — inline on the artifact path per the recorded deviation, the ontology's canonical evaluation exception.
A new version serves a slice before it serves everyone, and the previous promoted artifact stays loadable — rollback is a registry operation, not a re-download.
One governed front door for every caller: routing, admission and policy at a single crossing.
Workload identity per calling tenant, issued by the platform rather than a shared key in a config map.
Per-tenant quotas on finite capacity, enforced at admission rather than discovered at saturation.
Content and injection classification on both legs, because no provider is applying policy for you.
Reviewed serving configuration — batching, cache sharing, tenancy flags — treated as security settings, not tuning knobs.
Tenant-scoped cache keys, so a prefix hit can never cross a tenant boundary.
Hardware-backed isolation for the highest-sensitivity tenants where shared accelerators are not acceptable.
Track and patch the serving stack's CVE stream on your own schedule, because nobody upstream will.
Encryption, access control and integrity digests on weights at rest, matched by verification at load.
Continuous posture over which versions serve where and at what configuration, catching drift before an incident does.
Runtime weight and adapter updating disabled, and the control endpoints outside the versioned API unreachable from any tenant — the serving stack's own security guide says as much.
The distributed serving plane talks between nodes with no authentication by design; network isolation of that plane is the control, absorbed by platform network policy per the recorded deviation.

deviations.reason: The accelerators, the batch and the KV cache are internals of the inference runtime — the same block the endpoint architecture draws — so they appear as items inside it rather than as blocks, and the multi-tenancy risks pin to the runtime and its serving path.

deviations.reason: No MCP, tool or skills traffic exists on this drawing, so the gateway lists its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack — the same honesty rule the SaaS drawings and the MCP publisher apply in the other direction.

archetypes.title: Fine-tuning and model registry pipeline
summary: A build system whose artifact is a model. Curated data goes in, a tuned checkpoint comes out, and everything that is true of a compiler and its supply chain is true here — except that the output cannot be diffed and the defects cannot be found by reading it.
description:
Treating this as a build pipeline is the whole of the correct framing. It has source inputs, a build environment, dependencies, an artifact, a registry and a promotion path, and it deserves the controls a software pipeline gets: reproducibility, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses. Where the analogy breaks is inspection: a compiled binary can be decompiled and diffed; a tuned checkpoint cannot be read for backdoors in any practical sense. Input control and evaluation are the substitutes for code review — what went into the training set and how the result behaves are the only two things anyone can actually examine.
Poisoning is therefore the primary risk and it is durable. A poisoned example influences every inference the model ever makes, survives redeployment, and is not removable without retraining — and the dose is small: published results show a near-constant few hundred poisoned documents backdoor models regardless of scale, so poisoning needs a foothold, not a percentage. A targeted poisoning that only activates on a trigger phrase is invisible to accuracy metrics and to any evaluation that does not know what to look for — which is why curation is the last place a bad example can be removed rather than baked in, and why lineage from every promoted model back to its exact dataset is what makes a discovered poisoning scopeable at all.
Training data is also a disclosure surface in a way inference data is not. Memorised examples can be extracted from the model afterwards, so restricted-access content in the corpus becomes part of an artifact served far more widely than the dataset ever was. The two access questions to settle early: who may promote a checkpoint to production, and who may read the corpus. Both default to a broad platform-team role, and both are higher-privilege than they look — which is why promotion is a separated human decision and the signing key lives outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output.
distinguishedBy:
Against an ordinary data or software build pipeline: same trust properties, different artifact. A dataset or binary can be corrected in place and diffed; a model cannot — which is why the evaluation gate and the promotion decision carry the weight code review carries elsewhere.
Against self-hosted inference: that consumes artifacts, this produces them. They meet at the model registry this drawing now shows, and the promotion gate in front of it is where both archetypes' supply-chain controls concentrate.

exemplars.name: Axolotl
exemplars.note: Self-operated adapter and full fine-tuning on the organisation's own accelerators — the training-job tier of this drawing, run against a corpus and base checkpoint the organisation curates itself.

exemplars.name: MLflow Model Registry
exemplars.note: Versioned artifacts with lineage, stage transitions, approvals and rollback — the registry-and-promotion tier, operated beside whatever produced the checkpoint.

exemplars.name: Hugging Face PEFT
exemplars.note: Lightweight tuning producing an adapter rather than a full checkpoint. Smaller artifact, same supply-chain questions, and an additional one — who may load an adapter at serve time — that this page pins at the registry. Provider-hosted managed tuning is a different custody model and is deliberately not an exemplar here.

zones.note: Where the two inputs come from — the corpora we did not author and the base checkpoint we did not train. Drawn on the left because this is an ingest architecture: the outside world is its source, not its destination.
zones.title: External

zones.note: The build system end to end: the mirror that admits upstream artifacts, the curation stage, the assembled dataset, the GPU pool, the candidate store, and the evaluation and registry tiers that stand between a new checkpoint and anything that serves it.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Sparse, and deliberately. The dataset's provenance and the output's signature are the two things that make a run auditable six months later; the rest of an MLOps platform is a different architecture.

blocks.title: Base model & deps
blocks.note: The starting checkpoint and the frameworks around it, pulled from a public hub or an internal mirror. One of the run's two inputs, and the one whose format decides whether loading it is deserialization or execution.

items.label: Base checkpoint
items.note: The weights the run starts from — open, or one of our own earlier outputs.

items.label: Frameworks & dependencies
items.note: The training stack itself, and an ordinary software supply chain with model-shaped consequences.

blocks.title: Training content origins

items.label: Scraped & purchased sets
items.note: Content authored by people who did not know it would train a model.

items.label: Internal records
items.note: Our own data, and the reason the dataset store is the most sensitive thing on this page.

items.label: Human labels & preferences
items.note: Labels and preference judgements steer behaviour directly, and the workforce that writes them typically gets no scrutiny relative to that influence.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation-maintained mirror where base checkpoints and training frameworks are admitted before any job may pull them — format policy and scanning run here, by a tier the job cannot bypass, which is what makes the intake control independent of the thing it protects.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: The base weights and dependencies a run may use — admitted, scanned, and pinned by digest.

blocks.title: Curation & filtering
blocks.note: The processing tier between raw origins and the versioned corpus — the last point at which a poisoned or improperly sourced example is a deletion rather than a retraining decision.

items.label: Quality & safety filters
items.note: What a pipeline calls "curation" — filtering jobs somebody runs and tunes.

items.label: Sensitive-content removal
items.note: Restricted-access content removed before it can be memorised into a wider-served artifact.

items.label: Provenance capture
items.note: Per-example source and licence, recorded at ingest because it cannot be reconstructed later.

blocks.title: Training corpus
blocks.note: The assembled, versioned dataset the run actually reads — an object-storage bucket or a shared filesystem, mounted by every worker. Access control and provenance here matter more than anything else in the drawing.

items.label: Dataset versions
items.note: The exact bytes a given run consumed, addressable after the fact or the run is unreproducible.

blocks.title: Training job
blocks.note: The GPU pool and the framework running on it. The technique decides the shape more than anything else does: a quantized low-rank run fits on a single node, while a full fine-tune needs sharded optimizer state across nodes and a high-bandwidth interconnect. Everything the job holds — the dataset, the base weights, the credentials it was handed — is in one blast radius for the hours it runs.

items.label: GPU compute
items.note: One node or many, gang-scheduled; the interconnect is what decides whether multi-node is viable.

items.label: Tuning run
items.note: Full fine-tune, or the low-rank techniques that collapse the same job onto far less hardware. RL and agentic recipes execute model-generated actions inside the job, so the sandbox is part of the build environment, not an afterthought.

items.label: Reproducibility record
items.note: Which data, which base, which code, which seed — recorded during the run, not reconstructed later.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Where the candidate lands, unsigned. For a low-rank run that is an adapter directory of megabytes rather than a model; for a full fine-tune it is a complete checkpoint. Nothing serves from here: a candidate becomes loadable only by passing the gate and being signed at promotion. Encryption over these bytes is our keys, managed from the governance band.

items.label: Model files
items.note: The new weights, or the adapter that layers over the base — candidates until promoted.

blocks.title: Evaluation & red teaming
blocks.note: The blocking gate in front of promotion — candidates flow through it, which is why it is a block here and a governance item on the agent drawings. With an artifact that cannot be read, how the result behaves is one of only two things anyone can examine; the benchmarks themselves are custody-controlled, because a gate whose answer key the candidate's authors can edit gates nothing.

items.label: Capability & safety evals
items.note: Task performance and the safety regressions benign fine-tuning measurably causes.

items.label: Backdoor probing
items.note: Trigger-phrase hunting — the only chance to catch a poisoning accuracy metrics cannot see.

items.label: Memorisation testing
items.note: Whether restricted corpus content can be extracted back out of the artifact.

blocks.title: Model registry
blocks.note: Version, lineage, stage, approval, signature and rollback — the promotion semantics the title promises, operated as its own tier. The artifact bytes stay in the store behind it; what lives here is the decision record that makes one of them loadable. This is where this drawing meets self-hosted inference.

items.label: Candidate checkpoints
items.note: Every artifact the pipeline produced, promoted or not.

items.label: Lineage metadata
items.note: Which data, which base, which run — the record that scopes a discovered poisoning.

items.label: Signed releases
items.note: Signed at promotion, by an identity the training job never holds, so the serving tier's load-time verification proves the gate was passed.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: What went in and what came out: the provenance of every example, the format check on the base checkpoint before a loader opens it, and the record tying an artifact to the run that produced it.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Who may read the dataset and who may authorise a run against it. The dataset is the sensitive asset here, not the model.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Signing keys for the output, and the credentials the job holds for its whole run.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The lineage record and the documentation that travel with an artifact — the only reason a question asked long after the run has an answer.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: A workload identity per run, minted for the dataset version it was approved against and structurally unable to sign — the identity is what makes the promotion gate independent of the thing it gates.

edges.label: content in
edges.note: Raw material from outside, entering the one stage where a bad example is still a deletion. Everything after this hop is versioned and, eventually, learned.

edges.label: filtered set
edges.note: What survives filtering, with provenance stamped per example, assembled into the named, versioned set the run will read.

edges.label: base weights & deps in
edges.note: The starting checkpoint and its frameworks arrive at the mirror, where format policy and scanning gate admission. For several formats opening the file is itself the execution event, which is why this check runs at a tier the job cannot skip.

edges.label: approved artifacts
edges.note: The job pulls only what the mirror admitted, pinned by digest.

edges.label: dataset read
edges.note: Every worker in the job reads the same set, which is what makes its access control load-bearing.

edges.label: candidate out
edges.note: The output artifact — a full checkpoint, or an adapter of a few megabytes — lands unsigned. The job holds no signing identity; what it writes is a candidate, not a release.

edges.label: candidate under test
edges.note: The gate loads the candidate the way a serving tier would, and probes what cannot be read.

edges.label: artifact digest
edges.note: The registry records the digest of the bytes the store holds; the signed release points at exactly that artifact and nothing else.

edges.label: promotion
edges.note: A passing candidate is promoted: a separated human decision, a signature from an identity the job never held, and a registry entry tying artifact to data, base and run.

risks.note: A poisoned example entering the pipeline. The injection point of the whole architecture, and the reason curation and provenance stand between origins and the corpus rather than being assumed.
Content that was never licensed, consented to, or cleared for this use, learned irreversibly.
The most sensitive artifact in the drawing, mounted by every worker in the job. Its access control matters more than anything else on this page.

A base checkpoint whose format executes on load, or a framework dependency that does. Publisher identity says nothing about what the artifact does when opened — which is what admission at the mirror exists to decide.
The job holds the dataset, the base weights and its own credentials at once, for hours. Whatever compromises the training container gets all three.
The output is the expensive thing and it is small — an adapter is megabytes. Egress from the artifact store deserves the attention a model-sized file would not attract.

A gate whose benchmarks the candidate's authors can read or edit gates nothing — and a targeted poisoning is invisible to any evaluation that does not know what to look for. Benchmark custody is the control the gate itself depends on.

Memorised examples can be extracted from the artifact afterwards, so restricted corpus content becomes part of something served far more widely than the dataset ever was. Memorisation testing here is where that surfaces before promotion does.
An adapter layers over a clean, verified base at serve time — a trojaned one rides the base's reputation. Who may register an adapter, and which base it is approved against, is decided here.
The registry is third-party software with its own CVE stream, sitting between the job and the internet; its proxying of upstream sources is a network path in its own right.
Format policy at the mirror is what makes this leg a deserialization: a digest-pinned pickle is still pickle, and the loader opens it as the job.

capabilities.note: Quality, safety and sensitive-content filtering at the drawn stage — the last point at which a bad example is removable rather than learned.
Where every example came from, recorded at ingest, because it cannot be reconstructed after training.
Where sensitive records are in scope, de-identification and privacy-preserving transforms run here — applicability is a data-classification decision, not a default.
Who may read the set, enforced at the store rather than trusted to the job.
Format and content inspection gating admission to the mirror — before any loader in the job opens the file, and independent of the job it protects.

An approved run specification names the dataset version a job may read — a person per run is not the target state on a pipeline-launched platform; the approval is on the spec, and the identity enforces it.

Adversarial training and safety-preserving recipes where the tune's use is safety-critical — the one stage where robustness can be built in rather than bolted on, with the evaluation gate measuring whether it held.
Promotion is a separated human decision — a different person, and a different credential, from anything the run itself held.

Sign at promotion, with the OpenSSF Model Signing spec and a Sigstore bundle, using an identity the training job never possesses — so a signature proves the gate was passed, not merely that a job finished.
The behavioural half of what substitutes for code review: capability, safety, backdoor and memorisation checks, blocking promotion rather than advising it.
Reads from the candidate store are scoped and logged like corpus reads — the answering control for exfiltration of an artifact small enough to walk out unnoticed.
Our keys over the candidate store and the checkpoints the run wrote on the way — managed here, enforced as storage encryption from this service.
The record tying this artifact to this data, this base and this run.
Who ran what against which data, retained long enough to answer a question nobody has asked yet.
What the artifact is and what it was trained on, travelling with it rather than living in a wiki.
Pulling and publishing as separate grants: jobs pull pinned artifacts, and publishing belongs to the build and admission pipeline, so a compromised run cannot use the registry as a staging area.
Deny-by-default egress from the job: the mirror, the corpus store and the artifact store are the whole allowlist. Absorbed by the compute platform's network policy per the recorded deviation.
The run's own workload identity, scoped to the approved dataset version and denied the promotion identity — the separation the whole drawing rests on.
A release withdrawn here fails load-time verification everywhere it serves — the lineage query names the artifacts, and the registry's stage transition is the stop.
Rollouts in an RL or agentic recipe execute what the model generates; that execution is contained inside the job's environment — absorbed by the compute platform per the recorded deviation.

walkthrough.title: A tuning run produces a promoted adapter
walkthrough.moves: Curated data and an admitted base checkpoint through GPU compute, evaluation and promotion, into a signed registry entry.

steps.label: raw content
steps.note: Raw content enters the filtering stage — the last point a bad example is a deletion.

steps.label: versioned set
steps.note: What survives is assembled into a named, versioned set with provenance per example.

steps.label: same set, checked grant
steps.note: Every worker reads the same set, on a grant that is checked at the store.

steps.label: pinned base & frameworks
steps.note: The job pulls the base checkpoint and frameworks from the mirror, pinned by digest — only what was scanned and admitted when it arrived from upstream, which the base-checkpoint scenario walks.

steps.label: unsigned candidate
steps.note: The candidate lands, unsigned — the job holds no signing identity.

steps.label: evaluation gate
steps.note: The gate loads the candidate and probes what cannot be read.

steps.label: promotion, signed
steps.note: A human promotes; the artifact is signed by an identity the job never held, and the registry entry ties it to its data, base and run.

scenarios.title: A poisoning is discovered months later

steps.label: provenance to batch
steps.note: The provenance record maps the poisoned examples back to the batch they arrived in.

steps.label: to dataset version
steps.note: And to the dataset version they were assembled into.

steps.label: to every run
steps.note: And forward to every run that read that version — which is why versioning is not bookkeeping.

steps.label: every candidate suspect
steps.note: Every candidate those runs wrote is now suspect.

steps.label: passed gate, still suspect
steps.note: Including the ones that passed the gate — a behavioural backdoor is what the probes may have missed.

steps.label: promoted artifacts withdrawn
steps.note: The lineage metadata identifies every artifact those runs promoted, and they are withdrawn.

scenarios.title: The base checkpoint is the attack

steps.label: tampered checkpoint
steps.note: A tampered checkpoint arrives — a format that executes on load, or weights carrying a trained-in backdoor. Format policy and scanning refuse the first class here.

steps.label: admitted bytes
steps.note: A behavioural backdoor survives scanning — the mirror admits bytes, not behaviour.

steps.label: backdoor carried forward
steps.note: The candidate carries the backdoor forward; tuning does not remove it.

steps.label: backdoor probing
steps.note: Backdoor probing is the last control with a chance — and only if the probes do not come from a benchmark set the attacker could study.

scenarios.title: A compromised job tries to promote its own output

steps.label: unsigned candidate
steps.note: The job writes a candidate it would like the world to serve. It cannot sign it.

steps.label: gate it cannot pass
steps.note: The only road to promotion runs through a gate the job has no credentials for.

steps.label: signed on human approval
steps.note: Signature and registry entry happen here, on a human approval — a candidate that skipped the gate has no signature, and the serving tier's load-time verification refuses it.

deviations.subject: The external band is drawn on the left
deviations.reason: Band order is left-to-right by convention; this drawing reverses it because it is an ingest architecture — the outside world is its source, not its destination, and the read order should follow the data.

deviations.subject: Evaluation is drawn inline
deviations.reason: Everywhere else in the catalogue evaluation is a governance item, because it gates change rather than data. Here candidates flow through the gate, so it is a block — the ontology's own canonical example of a locus that legitimately differs by architecture.

deviations.subject: Mixed-custody origins are drawn as one external block
deviations.reason: Internal records reach the corpus beside scraped and purchased sets, and a self-trained base checkpoint can arrive beside an open one. Both are drawn entering from the external band because the ingest treatment — curation, provenance, admission — is identical regardless of custody; splitting the origins by owner would double the ingest chain to say nothing new. The custody difference is carried in the item notes.

deviations.subject: Job egress and rollout containment are absorbed by the compute platform
deviations.reason: Deny-by-default egress from the training job and containment of the actions an RL or agentic recipe executes are both delivered by the platform the job runs on — its network policy and its execution environment — rather than by any block the drawing could name. The pins sit on the job because that is what they bound.

Anthropic — a small, near-constant number of samples poisons models of any size
OpenSSF Model Signing — standardised signing and provenance for model artifacts

archetypes.title: First-party coding & desktop agents
summary: The same engine as the vendored coding agents without the vendor: an open-source harness a developer installs from a community registry and runs with their own keys. The interaction model is identical; what is missing is every control the vendor column supplied — session credentials, managed settings, audit export, an owner-bound remote relay — and nothing replaces them by default.
description:
Architecturally this is the vendored coding agent with the vendor service column deleted. The harness, the tool surface, the memory layer and the untrusted-content ingress are the same drawing; the differences are custody and supply chain. Credentials are pasted, long-lived keys that sit in plaintext configuration in most of the harnesses; governance is files on the same disk the agent can edit; and the binary itself arrives through community package registries and marketplaces — the category's landmark incident is a compromised harness release published with stolen publisher tokens.
The target state routes every model and remote call through an AI gateway the organisation operates — the credential broker that vaults the key the user would otherwise paste, the egress allowlist, the audit tap. The common state has nothing at that crossing: the harness calls the provider directly and the only record is the provider's bill. The gateway is drawn because this catalogue draws architectures as they should be built; the deviation records the distance.
Remote control exists here too, with a weaker admission model than the vendor products. The harnesses ship server modes — a listening port on the machine, localhost by default, with auth ranging from a mandatory shared secret down to none at all — plus official mobile clients over relay tunnels, and a fast-growing ecosystem of chat bridges that put messaging-platform identity in front of the loop. None of it binds admission to an owner account the way the vendor relays do, which is why the remote surface here is drawn with the same seriousness as the personal agent's channels.
The software ships no governance of its own: no managed settings tier, no session audit export, no admin toggle for the remote surface. The governance band this drawing carries is therefore entirely the organisation's — services the target state adds around the harness, none of them supplied by the thing being governed. Where enterprise controls exist for this category they are bolt-on — managed configuration paths and enterprise policy services a team must adopt deliberately — and the sanctioned posture is something the organisation publishes, not something the software ships.
distinguishedBy:
Against the vendored coding agents: the same loop, the same tool surface, the same human-present default. What changes is custody — pasted keys instead of expiring session credentials, community registries instead of signed vendor channels, bearer secrets and platform identity instead of an owner-bound relay — and the absence of any control plane an administrator could switch on.
Against the personal autonomous agent: this one is still invoked by a present developer and scoped to a workspace, with no heartbeat and no ambient senders. But the drift is real and one-directional — server modes, chat bridges, scheduled recipes — and a deployed OSS harness that listens on channels and runs unattended has become the personal agent and should be read on that page.

exemplars.name: Terminal harnesses
exemplars.note: The opencode/Crush class: TUIs over a client/server core, with headless serve modes and web surfaces. The most popular open-source agents, and the clearest expression of the pattern.

exemplars.name: IDE-extension harnesses
exemplars.note: The Cline family and its forks: marketplace-distributed extensions plus emerging standalone cores. The distribution channel is the marketplace — which is also the attack surface the category's worst incident used.

exemplars.name: Desktop and mobile-remote harnesses
exemplars.note: Goose-class agents with desktop apps, server binaries, scheduled recipes, and an official mobile client over a relay tunnel — the furthest drift toward the personal agent's shape, and the category's strongest remote-admission model.

zones.note: The developer at the keyboard, and the phone, browser and chat surfaces they steer the session from when they are not.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The managed device, running a harness the developer installed themselves: the loop, its tool surface and its memory. Ours to manage and nobody's to support — its outbound routes are the brokered crossing and, in the common install, whatever the harness dials itself.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: Infrastructure we operate — the AI gateway that brokers every model and remote call, and the systems and data it admits the agent into. With no vendor column, this band is the only place a control can live.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company with no agreement — package registries, the open web, third-party SaaS.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band — including the external connections, whose reachability is itself a governed decision.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The surfaces that steer a session when the developer is not at the machine — and here nothing binds them to an owner. A serve port takes a shared secret at best, a relay tunnel takes whatever the harness was configured with, and a chat bridge takes whoever the platform admits. That absence, not the surfaces themselves, is the finding.

items.label: Phone & web apps
items.note: Web UIs the harness serves itself, and mobile clients reaching it over relay tunnels. No vendor account stands behind any of them.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: Community bridges put messaging-platform identity in front of the loop — admission becomes whoever the channel admits, which is the personal agent's model exactly.

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: Present, watching, and the approval gate for what matters — the property the whole archetype's posture rests on, and the one that unattended modes quietly remove.

blocks.title: Remote relay
blocks.note: What a phone actually reaches, in the target state: a tunnel the harness dialled out to, a purpose-built agent relay, or a chat platform bridging into the loop. It is drawn in the external band because it is somebody else's service — including, for one popular harness, a default community relay with no IP allowlisting that most users will never change. The alternative is worse rather than better: with no relay the phone connects straight to a listening port on the machine.

items.label: Tunnel service
items.note: Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel or ngrok in front of a harness that ships no transport auth of its own.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: A community bridge putting messaging-platform identity in front of the loop.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The installed application — the loop behind the terminal, editor or chat window, running as the user, with its built-in tools nested inside it. Unlike the vendor products it commonly does open a port of its own — localhost by default, and the thing exposure scans keep finding when that default is changed.

items.label: Local API server
items.note: The serve mode: a listening port with auth ranging from a mandatory shared secret to none at all. This archetype's defining exposure, and the reason its remote surface is drawn with the same seriousness as the personal agent's channels.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides the next edit, command or screen action from everything it has read.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the instruction, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out: to local servers in its native tools, and through the gateway's MCP brokerage to remote ones.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Agent-written notes and the rules files merged into every later session — on by default in several products, and repo-committed in all of them.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Agent-written notes loaded at the start of every session.

items.label: Rules & instructions
items.note: The AGENTS.md-class files — the repo-committed ones authored by whoever last committed.

items.label: Hooks & settings
items.note: Session-start hooks, permission rules and editor tasks that run as code when the project opens — the persistence a self-propagating package worm writes into an agent's configuration, not prose the loop reads but commands it executes.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The application's built-in tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: file and edit tools, the shell, the local MCP servers it spawns or attaches to, the sandbox for builds and tests, skills and computer use — running as the user on a machine that also holds their SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions. What these tools reach is drawn: memory files, the package mirror, the gateway's API brokerage, and the internet directly when a local server holds its own token.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write across the working tree and the user's documents.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution with the user's authority when it runs outside the sandbox.

items.label: Local MCP servers
items.note: Local MCP servers: child processes the harness spawns through npx or uv, or servers already running on the machine, holding the user's privileges and, often, their own API tokens in a config dotfile. Remote MCP servers are a different thing on this catalogue — reached through the gateway, drawn in Tool services — and the industry names them apart.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Where builds, tests and driven desktops run when isolation is on.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions and helpers, delivered from the mirror through the crossing — content that executes as instruction, versioned and pinned like code.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: The sharpest tool the harness can switch on: the agent drives the GUI and inherits every application already signed in.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The organisation-operated crossing that replaces the missing vendor column, and the only component in this drawing that can hold a control at all: the vault for the key the developer would otherwise paste, the registry of MCP servers, APIs and connectors it will broker, and the admission decision for the remote surface. Which build of the agent runs is the mirror's decision, reached by the native tools directly. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers; the checks are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own tool servers and service APIs — the same component as the endpoint's local surface and the external one, at a different band. What the agent is actually meant to reach, and what the gateway in front of it decides it may.

items.label: Remote MCP servers
items.note: Our own servers, listed in the catalogue the gateway enforces.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: Service APIs reached on grants the gateway issues, scoped to the developer.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The repositories, documents and systems of record behind our own tool servers. Ours, and still untrusted as input — many hands wrote the content, and none of them are authenticated.

items.label: Code & project docs
items.note: A repository is a document the attacker may have contributed to.

items.label: Tool config dotfile
items.note: The tool-server declaration that ships with the code — the most attacked artifact here.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Business systems reached under the developer's scope, never a standing service account.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Governed content stores reached through our connectors rather than the device's mounts.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: Where the vendor column used to be. This archetype's supply chain includes the agent itself: the harness, its extensions and its skills all arrive through community channels on publisher self-attestation, and a compromised release of a harness has already shipped once. The organisation-maintained mirror moves the review earlier; it does not remove the risk.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: Harness releases, extensions and skills — reviewed, pinned and mirrored before installation.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Third-party servers and connectors — the same component again, out where nobody we contracted with operates it. Admitted by assessment even when the service is free and unsupported, or refused at the crossing.

items.label: Remote MCP servers
items.note: Remote servers whose tool descriptions enter context as model input.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: Third-party service calls made on brokered, developer-scoped credentials.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API the gateway brokers directly — no vendor service stands between. The completion drives writes, commands and clicks.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Receives code, documents and screenshots; returns the plan.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: What the native tools reach on the open internet — the web, and third-party SaaS the developer has grants into — through the gateway's brokered tool services or, on the direct path, on their own. Package registries are not here: the mirror is what the tools pull from, and its public sources are drawn feeding it.

items.label: Web & APIs
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop, and the exfiltration path out.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Third-party accounts reached on standing grants that outlive the conversation.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: The IdP and device-posture plane deciding who may open a session at all, and on what machine — the binding that makes the enterprise agreement apply to this traffic.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Vaulted, short-lived, connector-scoped grants on our own keys — and keeping the developer's own keys and sessions out of the agent's reach.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The decisions the one crossing enforces per call — what may be reached, what may leave, and what it may cost. With no vendor console above it, this is the only tier where a policy can be made non-overridable by the developer running the agent.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which agents, connectors and servers are admitted, and pinned to which versions. This call-out carries more weight here than in any other drawing: the supply chain delivers the harness itself, through channels that have already shipped a compromised release.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Our gateway tap is the only session record there is — no vendor export exists to fuse with it — plus the discovery that finds the installs which never enrolled.

edges.label: away from the machine
edges.note: The same person, not at the keyboard — or, on a chat surface, not necessarily the same person.

edges.label: local session
edges.note: The direct path, and the one most developers use: the CLI, editor or desktop app on the machine, authorised by holding the machine. The same shape as the personal agent's local session — proximity is the authorisation, so device posture carries it.

edges.label: remote steering
edges.note: The phone reaches the relay, not the machine. Nothing we operate is on this hop, and the relay is a third party we did not contract with — for one popular harness, a community instance running on somebody's goodwill.

edges.label: dialled-out tunnel
edges.note: The tunnel and bridge shapes: a relay the harness dialled out to, or a chat bridge forwarding platform messages. Admission is a bearer secret at best — never an owner-bound account, and never our firewall, because a phone on a cell network reaches the machine without passing through the corporate network at all. The third shape — a direct connection to the listening port with no relay anywhere — traverses nothing drawable at all, and is carried as the exposure risk pinned on the harness.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: The file tools are how the loop reads and writes what it learns — memory files written by the agent, rules and instructions read back on the next task. Context assembly loads the same rules at session start, through the same files.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: The one general-purpose crossing: every model call and every remote tool call leave the endpoint here — in the target state. In the common install the model call goes straight out on a pasted key and never sees this tier.

edges.label: API & MCP calls via gateway
edges.note: A local server's or tool's own calls to remote MCP servers, APIs and connectors, brokered here on the gateway's registry of destinations and on credentials it injects. Package installs go to the mirror, and the direct path below is the one this brokerage exists to replace.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Inference on a credential the gateway brokers, rather than the long-lived key the developer would otherwise paste into a dotfile. With no vendor between them, this is the whole model path — and in the common install it does not cross the gateway at all.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: Harness, extension and skill releases pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest — never from a community channel. The endpoint's egress allowlist is what makes the mirror the only place the sandbox can fetch from; the AI gateway brokers model and tool calls and is not on this path.

edges.label: direct egress
edges.note: The common shape of a local MCP server and of a shell command: a process on the machine holding its own token and calling the SaaS, the API or the web itself — no gateway, no broker, and no record on our side. A tool reaching a public package index directly is this path too, and it is the one the mirror exists to close. What bounds it is the endpoint's egress policy and where the token lives; both are pinned here.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: The path the deployment exists for: our own servers and APIs, admitted by the catalogue and reached on grants scoped to the developer.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Repository reads, the writes that become pull requests, and business-system calls — recorded on our side of the boundary.

edges.label: brokered external calls
edges.note: Admission is the catalogue; every call carries a scoped, short-lived credential.

edges.label: action / returned content
edges.note: Registries, the web and third-party accounts — and whatever returns re-enters the loop as context.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: Source files, manifests, issue text and documents are unrelated paths into the same context window, none of which is the developer's instruction.

Memory files and rules are prose a later session treats as instruction — including rules committed by whoever last touched the repo, and the settings hooks the worm incidents wrote their persistence into.
Configuration admits the whole native tools and can arrive with the clone. Injecting into it and swapping it after approval are the disclosed paths.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and this is where it becomes the plan — file writes, commands and clicks all start as text the model returned.

Code, documents and screenshots leave the company here — usually more than the developer pictured sharing, and with no vendor tenancy in between, whatever the provider's default retention happens to be is the retention policy.

A remote channel is only as good as the account and device binding behind it; a stale login steering a machine full of credentials is an account-compromise blast radius — and here admission is a bearer secret at best, never an owner-bound account.

The mirror decides which build of the agent runs. A tampered or unpinned release is code execution as the developer, on a machine that also holds their keys — the category's landmark incident, not a hypothetical.
The machine also holds SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions; outside the sandbox nothing separates them from the agent's shell on the way out.
Dependencies and remote servers arrive on publisher self-attestation, and their descriptions and contents are read into context as model input.
Writes into systems of record from a loop whose plan nobody reviewed.

The serve mode is an agent-control transport listening on the machine: bound wider than localhost with a guessable or absent secret, whoever reaches the port drives the loop directly — this archetype's defining exposure, on a path that traverses no relay and nothing we operate.
A binary a developer can fetch without asking anyone. Unmanaged, it has no policy, no audit and no inventory entry — and that is the common case.
The gateway is a third-party tier with its own CVE stream — the LiteLLM backdoor shipped in a release — and here there is no vendor console to notice a gateway that has gone quiet.
A remote MCP transport intercepted or impersonated between the crossing and the server it admits — the tool result arrives from whoever holds the connection.
A scheduled or hosted session has no human to notice it looping; seat metering is the only meter, and the stop is the credential.

Hooks and settings are executed, not read: a session-start hook or folder-open task written into the agent's configuration is code execution as the developer on every launch — the persistence the CHAINDROP worm chose.

The path a phone-home takes: a shell command or a local server bundles a token, a file or a key into a request and sends it itself. Nothing of ours is on this hop unless the endpoint's egress policy is — and the token a local MCP server uses lives in a dotfile on the same disk.

capabilities.note: Bind the remote surface to a named user on a managed device by contracting the relay: a zero-trust tunnel tied to our directory is the only way this path acquires an identity we govern. Nothing in this category does it on its own — a serve port takes a shared secret, a chat bridge takes whoever the platform admits — and an uncontracted community relay leaves the path uncontrolled, which is then the finding.
Session admission and per-call policy evaluated at the edge, outside the application being governed.
Pin harness, extension and skill versions against the mirror; an update is a decision, because the update channel is this category's proven attack path.
Inspection belongs on the brokered tool path, where the agent's calls carry repository content out to servers we did not write — not on the pinned vendor session.
Spend ceilings at the crossing, because the only native meter in this category is the provider's invoice — there is no vendor console showing seat usage or session counts.
Per-tool grants scoped to the working tree and the task, instead of the developer's full authority on the machine — enforced where the tools run, inside the application.
Make sandboxed tools the default path for commands and computer use, so the approval gate fires only for actions that leave the box.
Keep SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profiles outside the agent's reachable filesystem.
Treat memory and rules as untrusted input on read; a repo-committed rules change is a code change.
Treat repository and document content as untrusted; it cannot be authenticated, only bounded.
The provider key lives in the gateway's vault, never pasted into a dotfile — and org access rides short-lived, connector-scoped grants the crossing issues per call.
Provenance and behavioural review before a server is admitted; pin versions so an update is a decision.
Non-overridable approval on consequential writes, kept rare enough that each prompt is read.
A managed allowlist of connectors and tool servers, enforced from our gateway rather than from the configuration file it governs.
The gateway tap is the whole record: with no vendor console anywhere, what does not cross here was never logged at all.
Find the installs that never enrolled, because this archetype spreads one developer at a time.

The device tooling that sees what no crossing can: which harnesses are installed, which ports they listen on, what their processes execute — and the containment that isolates a machine whose agent has been steered.

Admission of a remote instruction: the relay's identity headers and the harness's shared secret decide whether a steering message is executed — absorbed by the harness and the contracted relay, recorded as a deviation.
Revoke the brokered credential and block the port from device management — the only stop, because no vendor console exists.
Digest and signature verification at admission to the mirror, and an inventory of which harness, extension and skill builds are permitted to run.
Instruction files, hooks and settings are configuration and are managed as code: reviewed on change, diffed on clone, never executed from a package a dependency dropped in.

The endpoint's egress allowlist, enforced by device management, decides where the direct path may go: the AI gateway, the package mirror, and the named services a local server is approved to call — nothing else. Shell commands, fetches and browser traffic are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.
The gateway's own allowlist: which external MCP servers, APIs and peer agents are registered, and which tools each key may call on them. Configuration of a broker, not a network control.

Admission scanning at the mirror: digest and signature verification, malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.

walkthrough.title: The developer asks for a change
walkthrough.moves: A task stated at the machine, inference, and the approved edits and calls it produces.

steps.label: task stated
steps.note: The task is stated by a human who will stay for the session.

steps.label: model call, brokered
steps.note: The turn's model call crosses on a brokered credential — or, in the common install, does not cross here at all and goes straight out on a pasted key.

steps.label: inference on vaulted key
steps.note: Inference on the vaulted key, against an allowlisted provider.

steps.label: completion
steps.note: The completion comes back across the same brokered crossing.

steps.label: plan into loop
steps.note: And into the loop — unauthenticated content, now the plan.

steps.label: approval prompt
steps.note: Consequential actions surface for approval before they run — the only gate there is, kept rare enough that each prompt is read.

steps.label: approved (bound)
steps.note: Approved — this action, these arguments, not a blanket yes.

steps.label: edits, commands; brokered calls
steps.note: Edits and commands execute inside the application's native tools, with whatever scope the permission model granted. Anything a local tool sends to a remote server or connector crosses our tier here — brokered, on a credential the gateway injects.

steps.label: admitted third-party server
steps.note: A third-party server or connector, admitted by the catalogue on a scoped credential.

steps.label: action outside
steps.note: And out to what those services act on. What comes back is loaded and read as context, which is why the provenance of a tool matters as much as the content of a page.

steps.label: returned content
steps.note: What the service acted on returns — records, pages, API responses — authored by somebody else.

steps.label: classified result
steps.note: Across the crossing, where the return is classified before anything on the endpoint reads it.

steps.label: tool result into context
steps.note: Into the native tools as a tool result, and from there into context.

steps.label: the change, for review
steps.note: The change lands in the working tree for the developer to review — the loop's output is a diff, never a merge.

scenarios.title: Steering from a phone

steps.label: instruction from phone
steps.note: The developer types the instruction on a phone, a web UI the harness serves, or a chat thread.

steps.label: to third-party relay
steps.note: The phone reaches a third-party relay. Nothing we operate is on this hop, and for one popular harness the default is a community relay with no IP allowlisting.

steps.label: down dialled-out tunnel
steps.note: The relay hands the instruction down a connection the harness dialled out. Admission is a bearer secret at best; with no relay at all the phone connects straight to a listening port and admission is whatever that port checks, which is often nothing.

steps.label: result up the tunnel
steps.note: The result goes back up the same dialled-out connection.

steps.label: back to phone
steps.note: And back to the phone. The same shape as the third-party round trip, with a party in the middle that vouches for nothing — no owner account, no tenant, often no allowlist. That is the whole difference between the two drawings.

scenarios.title: A poisoned document phones home

steps.label: document request
steps.note: The loop asks for a document — a ticket, a wiki page, a shared file — through the crossing.

steps.label: brokered to connector
steps.note: Brokered to the connector that can read it.

steps.label: document with hidden instruction
steps.note: A hidden instruction in the document is read along with the document.

steps.label: content as tool result
steps.note: The content comes back as a tool result.

steps.label: back across crossing
steps.note: Across the crossing, where inspection is possible and rarely configured.

steps.label: into context
steps.note: And into context, where the loop cannot tell the instruction from the task.

steps.label: poisoned context for inference
steps.note: The poisoned context goes up for inference.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: Nothing on this hop knows the context is hostile.

steps.label: attacker's plan
steps.note: The completion carries the attacker's instruction as the plan.

steps.label: next step
steps.note: The loop treats it as the next step.

steps.label: exfil on direct egress
steps.note: A shell command or a local server bundles a token, a file or a key into a request and sends it itself — the direct path, where the endpoint's egress allowlist is the last control standing, and on the common install there is none.

scenarios.title: The harness updates itself

steps.label: release pull (pinned)
steps.note: A new release of the harness or one of its extensions is requested — the package manager runs as the developer, in the application's own tools, on the supply chain's proven path, straight to the mirror: the one destination the egress allowlist permits, and where a version is pinned and a review has happened.

steps.label: approved build
steps.note: The approved build comes back, digest-checked against the pin — the hop a compromised release actually arrives on — and loads into the running process with everything the agent has. A compromised release is code execution as the developer.

deviations.subject: There is no vendor band
deviations.reason: That absence is the archetype. Every control the vendor column supplied in the third-party drawing — expiring session credentials, managed settings, session audit export, an owner-bound remote relay — has no counterpart here, and nothing replaces them by default. The family differs in exactly three places, all consequences of the missing column: custody (a Remote relay in the external band where the vendor's owner-bound relay stood, plus the listening serve port), the software supply chain (the Private pkg registry, because the community channel delivers the agent itself), and the spend meter (a rate-limiting pin, because no vendor console exists). Everything else is deliberately identical so a reader comparing the two sees those differences and nothing else.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway is drawn although the common install lacks it
deviations.reason: This catalogue draws target states. The gateway is the organisation's replacement for the missing vendor column — key vault, egress policy, audit, and the admission decision for the remote surface — and the common state, a pasted key calling the provider directly, is recorded here rather than drawn as a second model path.

deviations.subject: The private package registry is drawn in the enterprise band, not as a tool source
deviations.reason: In this archetype the registry delivers the agent itself, not merely what the agent calls. Drawing it in the enterprise band rather than out among the downstream services says the thing that matters: which build of the harness is permitted to run is a decision the organisation makes at its own mirror, which the native tools reaches directly under the endpoint's egress allowlist.

deviations.subject: The sandbox is a Sandboxed tools item, not a frame
deviations.reason: Of the ontology's three canonical sandbox forms, this one is a contained execution path inside one application: the harness and shell run as the user, and only tool execution is contained — conditionally, when isolation is on. A boundary frame would claim a containment the drawing's own notes deny. The personal agent, whose whole loop lives inside the container, draws the frame; here the item form is the honest one.

deviations.subject: Identity governance and remote admission are absorbed by the relay and the harness
deviations.reason: Two inline pins sit on components that are not their registered embodiment. Identity governance on the relay is delivered by contracting a zero-trust tunnel tied to our directory — an uncontracted community relay leaves the pin unmet, which is then the finding. Runtime enforcement on the relay-to-harness hop is the harness's own shared secret and loopback bind plus the relay's identity headers; nothing else on this path can hold it.
