tools.name: Claude Managed Agents

variants.name: Managed Agents API (agents, environments, sessions, vaults) on api.anthropic.com
Self-hosted sandboxes (your worker polls the environment work queue)
variants.note: Control plane stays with Anthropic; sandbox image, egress, service-key custody and session-content retention are yours. Environment-variable vault credentials are not yet supported here.

summary: Anthropic's hosted agent harness (beta; every request carries the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header, enabled by default for API accounts): you define an agent (model, system prompt, toolset, MCP servers, skills), an environment (Anthropic cloud sandbox — an isolated Ubuntu container, up to 8 GB / 10 GB — or a self-hosted sandbox), then run sessions that stream events over SSE. The sandbox runs bash, file tools and code; web_search and web_fetch run on Anthropic's servers. Sessions are stateful: event history persists until you delete the session and sandbox state is checkpointed for 30 days, so Managed Agents is not ZDR- or HIPAA-BAA-eligible.

Governance is API-native and workspace-scoped: permission_policy always_allow / always_ask per toolset or per tool (MCP toolsets default to always_ask), tool enable flags, per-tool allowed_domains / blocked_domains, environment networking unrestricted / limited with allowed_hosts, vault credentials injected at egress so the agent never sees the secret, hard dollar session budgets, versioned agent definitions, memory stores with immutable version history and redaction, signed webhooks and a persisted event stream. Also available on Claude Platform on AWS with differences.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Any Claude API organisation (beta, on by default); MCP tunnels and dreaming are a limited research preview. Billed per model token, $10 per 1,000 web searches and $0.08 per session hour at list rates.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Anthropic API only (plus Claude Platform on AWS); model pinned per agent with optional inference_geo "us" validated against the workspace's allowed_inference_geos.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Everything runs on Anthropic infrastructure: conversation, tool inputs/outputs, files and sandbox state; self-hosted sandboxes keep tool execution and files on your side while the transcript still passes through Anthropic.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Commercial terms (no training). Session transcripts persist until you delete the session; sandbox checkpoints 30 days; memory versions retained 30 days (recent versions longer); not eligible for ZDR or HIPAA BAA.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents (overview through reference)

riskNotes.note: Vaults and credentials are workspace-scoped: any API key with workspace access can reference them at session creation, and the docs recommend separate workspaces and environments per trust boundary for self-hosted sandboxes.

Memory stores attach read_write by default and the docs warn a successful injection can write content later sessions read as trusted; use read_only for reference stores and limited networking with allowed_hosts for production.

The built-in agent toolset defaults to always_allow, including bash with unrestricted egress on API-created environments; production guidance is limited networking and always_ask on bash or MCP tools that write.

MCP servers are declared by URL with no allowlist beyond the agent definition; MCP toolsets default to always_ask so newly added server tools do not run unapproved, and per-tool enabled flags can pin the set.

Custom tool results, uploaded files and outputs are stored server-side until deleted; OAuth exchanges performed inside the sandbox return tokens unredacted, so perform exchanges outside and store the result in the vault.

controls.mechanism: Claude Console organisation and workspace membership, roles, SSO/SCIM and API-key or workload identity federation credentials gate who can create agents and sessions

steps.title: Scope operators by workspace
body: Create agents, environments and vaults in a dedicated Console workspace and issue keys (or a WIF service account) scoped to it; Console SSO and SCIM govern the humans.

controls.mechanism: Agent resources with ids and versions; per-session vault identity (display_name and metadata mapping to your user); environment service keys and per-session secrets for self-hosted workers; no cryptographic agent identity presented to third parties

steps.title: Bind each session to an end-user vault
body: Create one vault per end user (metadata external_user_id) and pass vault_ids at session creation so actions on MCP servers are attributable to that user's credentials.

steps.title: Protect the environment key
body: Store ANTHROPIC_ENVIRONMENT_KEY in a secrets manager, pass the per-session secret only into the sandbox serving that session, and revoke on suspicion (validated on every request).

controls.mechanism: Vault credentials (mcp_oauth with managed refresh, static_bearer, environment_variable with networking.allowed_hosts and injection_location) substituted at egress; secret values are write-only; rotate via update, archive purges the secret

steps.title: Register credentials in a vault
body: Add mcp_oauth or static_bearer credentials keyed by mcp_server_url, or environment_variable credentials keyed by secret_name with networking type limited and allowed_hosts; the agent sees only an opaque placeholder.

steps.title: Rotate and revoke
body: Update the credential's secret (running sessions re-resolve without restart), archive to purge the secret while keeping the audit record, and subscribe to vault_credential.refresh_failed webhooks.

controls.mechanism: Anthropic infrastructure encryption; inference_geo pinning; no customer-managed keys for Managed Agents session storage

steps.title: Pin inference geography
body: Set model.inference_geo "us" on the agent; it is validated against the workspace's allowed_inference_geos on save, at session creation and on every turn.

controls.note: CMEK is documented for Claude Enterprise data, not for Managed Agents sessions or memory stores.

controls.mechanism: Agents are first-class workspace resources with id, name, description, metadata, version history, archive; environments, vaults, memory stores and deployments likewise; list endpoints and lifecycle webhooks

steps.title: Treat the agent resource as the registry
body: Create agents once with metadata for ownership, list versions, and archive retired agents (new sessions cannot reference them); subscribe to agent.created / updated / archived webhooks.

controls.mechanism: Agent version increments on every change with optimistic concurrency (version field, 409 on mismatch), full version history, coordinator rosters pinned to a version; sessions keep the configuration they started with

steps.title: Roll forward and back by version
body: Update with the version field for safe concurrent edits, list versions to audit, and re-apply an earlier configuration to roll back; environments are not versioned, so keep your own record.

controls.mechanism: agent_toolset_20260401 default_config / configs with enabled false per tool, MCP toolset per-tool enabled flags, web_search / web_fetch allowed_domains or blocked_domains, permission_policy per tool

steps.title: Enable only the tools the agent needs
body: Set default_config.enabled false and enable bash, read, write and so on individually; do the same on mcp_toolset entries so server-added tools stay off.

steps.title: Restrict the web tools
body: Put allowed_domains or blocked_domains on the web_search and web_fetch config entries (up to 64 domains each); environment networking does not govern these tools.

controls.mechanism: permission_policy always_ask pauses the session (session.status_idle with requires_action) until a user.tool_confirmation allow/deny event; custom tools always return to your application; webhooks notify on session.status_idled

steps.title: Require confirmation for risky tools
body: Set permission_policy type always_ask on the agent toolset (or on bash alone via configs) and on MCP toolsets (the default); answer with user.tool_confirmation including a deny_message.

controls.mechanism: Model-side safeguards plus structural limits: limited networking, read_only memory stores, always_ask policies and domain lists; no configurable injection classifier

steps.title: Contain the blast radius
body: Use networking type limited with allowed_hosts, attach reference memory stores as read_only, and keep MCP toolsets on always_ask when the agent processes untrusted input.

controls.mechanism: Anthropic Trust Center artifacts and the API data-retention page feed the buyer's TPRM platform

steps.title: Record the retention posture
body: Managed Agents is stateful and not ZDR- or HIPAA-eligible; capture this from the retention page in the vendor assessment.

controls.mechanism: Persisted session event stream (agent.tool_use / tool_result / mcp_tool_use / message, span.model_request_start/end with usage, session.error, thread events) over SSE and list endpoints; session.usage snapshots

steps.title: Consume and archive the event stream
body: Stream events per session (open the stream before sending), and list past events by type for reconstruction; every persisted event has an id and processed_at.

controls.mechanism: Full event history persisted with the session until deletion; memory version history attributed to sessions; vault archive keeps records after purging secrets; signed webhooks (webhook-signature, 5-minute freshness)

steps.title: Keep an off-platform copy
body: Webhooks are not a durable log (three attempts, then dropped); reconcile by listing session events and export memory versions before the 30-day window expires.

controls.note: The event history is customer-deletable and not tamper-evident in the Five Eyes sense; your archive is the record.

controls.mechanism: Anthropic's model safety systems (content blocks can be redacted by model policy); web tool domain lists; no organisation-level content filter applies to Managed Agents sessions

steps.title: Note what the Console settings do not cover
body: Organisation-level web search and fetch settings in the Console apply to the Messages API only; configure allowed_domains / blocked_domains on the toolset instead.

controls.mechanism: Memory stores are workspace-scoped resources attached per session with access read_write or read_only, capped at 8 per session; every write creates an immutable version; versions can be redacted; stores can be archived or deleted

steps.title: Segment and scope stores
body: Use one store per user, team or project, attach shared reference stores read_only, and pass instructions per attachment.

steps.title: Audit and roll back memory
body: List memory versions, restore prior content by writing it back, and redact versions that captured secrets or PII while keeping the audit trail.

controls.mechanism: Outcome-driven sessions run a grader that evaluates iterations against a defined outcome; no release-gate eval harness

steps.title: Use outcomes as an in-session check
body: Send user.define_outcome so a grader (without web tools) evaluates each iteration and emits span.outcome_evaluation_end with satisfied / needs_revision / failed.

controls.mechanism: Agent, environment, vault and deployment listings plus webhooks feed the organisation's governance system of record

steps.title: Sync the inventory
body: Poll the list endpoints or subscribe to agent, environment, vault and deployment webhooks to mirror owners, versions and archive state into your governance platform.

controls.mechanism: Session budget (type limit, max_list_cost in USD cents) enforced between model requests, budgets copied onto deployment runs, organisation spend limits and usage-tier rate limits, per-org create/read request limits

steps.title: Cap each session and deployment
body: Pass budget.max_list_cost at session creation (cannot be added later); a session at its cap goes idle with budget_reached and accepts only settle events until the cap is raised or removed.

controls.mechanism: user.interrupt, session archive and delete (removes events and sandbox), agent archive (blocks new sessions), vault or credential archive/delete (purges secrets, propagates to running sessions), environment key revocation, deployment pause

steps.title: Stop and decommission
body: Send user.interrupt, then archive or delete the session; archive the agent so no new sessions start; archive vault credentials to revoke access (running sessions re-resolve credentials periodically).

controls.mechanism: Every configuration is readable through the API (agents, environments, vaults minus secrets, memory stores, deployments) for posture checks

steps.title: Check posture from the API
body: Enumerate environments for networking type unrestricted, agents for always_allow bash or missing domain lists, and sessions without budgets; treat these as findings.

variants.name: @Claude in Slack channels (organisation agent identity)
@Claude direct messages (runs on the member's own claude.ai account)
variants.note: DMs use the member's personal connectors and seat; Owners can disable DMs organisation-wide.

variants.name: Claude Code in Slack (earlier per-user version; Pro/Max, retiring on Team/Enterprise)

summary: Claude Tag is Anthropic's organisation-managed @Claude for Slack (public beta on Team and Enterprise, first-party service only, not for ZDR organisations). In channels Claude acts under its own service accounts that an Owner provisions, not as the person who tagged it; each thread runs in an ephemeral sandbox on the same infrastructure as Claude Code on the web (or in a self-hosted environment), and every outbound request crosses Agent Proxy, which injects credentials from a write-only store and blocks hosts no allow layer covers. Direct messages instead run on the sender's own claude.ai account with their personal connectors.

Admin control lives at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag (Owner role): pairing workspaces, Access bundles of credentials, repository grants, domains, plugins and instructions attached per scope (organisation, workspace or channel), the "Enable Claude Tag for your organization" toggle, per-scope version Off, member and guest restrictions, blocked channel patterns, DM toggle, auto-mode allow rules, and spend limits at claude.ai/admin-settings/usage/claude-tag. Channel work bills to the organisation's usage balance. Session transcripts, channel and workspace memory, routines and artifacts are stored by Anthropic with no automatic retention period during the beta and are not yet in the Compliance API session endpoints.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Team and Enterprise only; not on Free, Pro, Max, third-party deployments or ZDR organisations. Routines must be enabled at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-code. Slack Connect (externally shared) channels are never served.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Anthropic first-party API from Anthropic-managed sandboxes; self-hosted environments run the sandbox on your runners but still call api.anthropic.com.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Slack messages Claude is shown (including other people's and guests'), attached files, Slack search results, data retrieved from connected tools and everything Claude did are held as session transcripts on Anthropic's side; web search runs on Anthropic's servers outside Agent Proxy rules.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: No automatic retention period during the beta; custom organisation retention does not apply to transcripts or memory (it does to artifacts); deletion is by disconnecting a workspace, removing a channel scope, deleting memory files or routines, or uninstalling the app. Commercial terms (no training).

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: claude.com/docs/claude-tag (concepts, admins, users)

riskNotes.note: Anyone in a channel under a bundle's scope can make Claude act with that bundle's credentials; the docs say to connect a dedicated service account per tool, attach narrow bundles to private channels, and never a personal login.

Claude reads whole threads and can respond without being tagged; guests' and other members' messages become instructions and transcript content. Auto-mode allow rules pre-approve actions per scope, and there is no per-thread deny list.

Public-channel memory is shared workspace-wide and survives a channel going private; Claude can keyword-search public channels without being added to them; artifacts are readable by anyone with access to the source channel.

On an Enterprise Grid paired to several Claude organisations, one organisation's access settings govern the whole grid; bundle isolation comes from where a bundle is attached, not from the bundle itself.
Routines and channel watches run unattended with the channel's credentials and are created by any channel member; the Audit page's Scheduled work tab is the inventory.

controls.mechanism: Owner-only setup and configuration; "Restrict to roles with Claude Tag access" (Enterprise custom roles with the Claude Tag in Slack capability) or "Restrict to your organization" (Team); "Restrict to your verified domains" for account linking; channel managers via custom roles

steps.title: Restrict who can invoke Claude
body: At claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag > Where Claude Tag works > Member access, turn on "Restrict to roles with Claude Tag access" (Enterprise) or "Restrict to your organization" (Team); the toggle covers channels and DMs.

steps.title: Gate by custom role
body: Create groups at claude.ai/admin-settings/groups and a custom role at claude.ai/admin-settings/roles with the "Claude Tag in Slack" capability; built-in roles always grant it.

controls.mechanism: Corporate proxy tenant-restriction header for claude.ai; Slack-side app approval and Enterprise Grid distribution controls
controls.note: Claude Tag runs server-side, so the only network-layer levers are the Slack admin's app approval and the anthropic-allowed-org-ids header on claude.ai traffic for the account linking flow.

steps.title: Control the Slack side
body: Slack workspace admins decide whether the Claude app is installed; on Enterprise Grid, org admins choose which workspaces get it; removing the app revokes access immediately.

controls.mechanism: Default-deny egress through Agent Proxy (data leaves only to allowed hosts); credentials never enter the sandbox; Enterprise Inference hooks are not documented for Claude Tag

steps.title: Keep egress default-deny
body: Leave the environment at Trusted or pin a No access environment on the scope, list only needed hosts on the bundle's Domains tab, and do not request allow-all egress unless required.

controls.note: No content inspection of prompts or outputs is offered; artifact publishing and Slack posting are the visible egress paths.
Not applicable: the surface is Slack and a server-side sandbox, not a browser session the organisation instruments.

controls.mechanism: Agent Proxy allow layers: connection allowed websites (credentialed), bundle Domains tab (uncredentialed, wildcard leftmost label, ports), and the scope's environment network access level (Trusted default, Custom, Full, No access); private ranges and cloud metadata always blocked; HTTP/HTTPS only

steps.title: Allow hosts per bundle
body: On the bundle's Domains tab add each hostname (and non-443 ports); requests to unlisted hosts are blocked and Claude names the blocked host in the thread.

steps.title: Pin a stricter environment on the scope
body: Create an organisation-shared cloud environment with No access or a Custom list and choose it under the scope's Advanced > Environment.

controls.mechanism: Audit page (Scheduled work, Memory, Network events export), Access bundles page with per-connection status, analytics at claude.ai/analytics/claude-tag

steps.title: Inventory what Claude can do and does
body: Review the Access bundles page (Active / Never used per credential), the Audit page tabs at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag/audit, and the per-channel Access summary.

controls.mechanism: Sessions run in auto mode (classifier); Owners add narrow auto-mode allow rules per scope; pull requests are drafts for humans to merge; "Respond automatically" per channel

steps.title: Keep allow rules narrow
body: Add auto-mode allow rules only on the narrowest scope (up to 50 per scope, 1,024 characters each) and name the tool, action and environment; everything else stays under the classifier.

steps.title: Stop proactive work where it is not wanted
body: Turn off a channel's Respond automatically setting so Claude only works when tagged; proactive sessions bill under Proactive.

controls.note: There is no per-action approval prompt in a channel; the classifier and deny-by-egress are the gates.

controls.mechanism: Auto-mode classifier plus structural containment (credential-free sandbox, default-deny egress, service-account scoping)

steps.title: Contain rather than detect
body: Attach bundles holding sensitive credentials only to private channels, keep guest channels Restricted, and rely on Agent Proxy blocking unlisted hosts.

controls.mechanism: Claude acts under provisioned service accounts (Slack app, Claude GitHub App, one dedicated account per connected tool) so actions are attributable in each tool's audit log; DMs use the member's identity

steps.title: Provision a dedicated identity per tool
body: Create a mailbox such as claude@yourcompany, add it to each tool with the narrowest role, and paste that account's API key on the setup page; rotate or delete from the bundle's Credentials tab.

controls.mechanism: Admin console readback (Access bundles, scopes, Access summary), audit log entries for channel-manager and deletion actions via the Compliance API Activity Feed

steps.title: Evidence the configuration
body: Export the channel Access summary and bundle listings, and read channel-manager credential changes and scope removals from the organisation audit log through the Compliance API.

controls.mechanism: Memory files viewable, editable and deletable per scope by Owners; data lifecycle table for every deletion action; no retention window during beta

steps.title: Review and prune memory
body: Open a scope's View memory files (or the Audit page Memory tab) to read, edit or delete what Claude saved; workspace memory from public channels is shared workspace-wide.

steps.title: Delete data deliberately
body: Removing a channel scope deletes its sessions, memory, routines and artifacts; disconnecting the workspace deletes everything for that workspace; version Off deletes nothing.

controls.mechanism: Anthropic Trust Center artifacts plus the security-and-data and data-lifecycle pages feed the buyer's vendor assessment

steps.title: Record beta-specific gaps
body: Note in the vendor record that transcripts and memory have no retention period, are excluded from data exports and Compliance API sessions during the beta, and that ZDR organisations are excluded.

controls.mechanism: Credentials kept in a separate write-only credential store and injected at the proxy; Anthropic infrastructure encryption; no CMEK documented for Claude Tag data

steps.title: Understand where credentials live
body: Saved credentials are never displayed again and travel only to the hosts named on the connection; narrow to host, path prefix or read-only methods.

controls.mechanism: Access bundle credentials (Bearer, Basic, AWS SigV4, GCP service account, OAuth client credentials, MCP Connector sign-in) injected by Agent Proxy; rotate secret and setup links for another admin to submit a secret

steps.title: Add and rotate credentials in bundles
body: On the bundle's Credentials tab connect each service, set Allowed hosts, restrict by HTTP method or path, and use Rotate secret; use "Copy link for another admin" so the secret owner submits it directly.

controls.mechanism: Per-scope Access bundles (credentials, repositories, plugins, instructions) with inheritance from Default Slack to workspace to channel; connection host/path/method restrictions; plugin enable toggles per bundle

steps.title: Compose access by capability and channel
body: Create bundles such as data-readonly, github-write and monitoring, attach only what a channel needs, and keep sensitive bundles on private channels.

steps.title: Narrow each connection
body: Edit a connection to restrict it to specific hosts, a path prefix and read-only methods, and scope the underlying service account to the projects it needs.

controls.mechanism: Reach inside a tool equals what the service account can access; account-level scoping is the control; DMs run as the user

steps.title: Scope the service account, not just the connection
body: Share only the folders, spaces or projects Claude should see with its dedicated account; host and path rules limit endpoints, not records.

controls.mechanism: Scopes and bundles are the registry of where Claude runs and with what; Scheduled work tab lists every routine with Created by

steps.title: List where Claude operates and what is scheduled
body: The Slack tab under Claude Tag's access lists workspaces and channels with their bundles; the Audit page Scheduled work tab lists routines with pause and delete.

controls.mechanism: Audit page (routines, memory, hourly Network events JSON export of Agent Proxy calls, excluding git and MCP), attribution under service accounts in each tool's logs, organisation audit log via Compliance API for channel-manager and deletion events

steps.title: Download network events and read tool-side logs
body: Export hourly Network events from claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag/audit and correlate with the service account's entries in GitHub, Datadog and other tools.

controls.note: Session transcripts are not exportable and the Compliance API does not list Claude Tag sessions during the beta.

controls.mechanism: Blocked and auto-join channel name patterns; Claude responds only where added; per-scope version Off; Slack app inventory

steps.title: Fence channels by name
body: Add Blocked channel patterns (for example *-confidential-*) under Default Slack access > Advanced so Claude stays silent even if invited.

controls.mechanism: Enable Claude Tag for your organization toggle, per-scope Claude Tag version Off, Allow direct messages off, /remove @Claude, bundle deletion (revokes credentials everywhere), workspace disconnect, app uninstall, spend limit reached

steps.title: Stop responding and revoke credentials
body: Set the scope's version to Off (or the org toggle), then delete the bundle to revoke its credentials; running sessions may hold a revoked credential briefly.

steps.title: Decommission the data
body: Disconnect the workspace at claude.ai/admin-settings/claude-tag to delete its sessions, memory, routines, artifacts and account links.

summary: Cloud Agents (formerly Background Agents) run the Cursor agent in a Firecracker microVM in a dedicated AWS account, one VM boundary per agent rather than a shared process sandbox. They clone repositories through a Cursor GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket / Azure DevOps app an account admin connected, work on a branch and hand back a draft pull request. Triggers are the web app, iOS, the Desktop Cloud dropdown, @cursor in Slack, Linear, GitHub or Bitbucket, the Cloud Agents API (public beta) and Automations that fire on schedules, source-control, Slack, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty or webhook events. Bugbot, Security Agents and Approval Agents are Cloud Agents wired to pull-request events; Self-Hosted Machines move tool execution onto customer workers while the agent loop and inference stay in Cursor's cloud.

Inference runs on Cursor's hosted providers under Privacy Mode (Cloud Agents do not support Legacy Privacy Mode and never train on accessed code). Code is stored temporarily while a run executes; conversation state is retained indefinitely by default until deleted, VM snapshots are deleted after 90 days idle. Data at rest is AES-256 with per-agent keys, TLS 1.2+ in transit, and Enterprise teams can bring a customer-managed KMS key (CMEK/BYOK). Egress leaves from published CIDR ranges (docs/ips.json) and a fixed three-IP git proxy; AWS PrivateLink or Cloudflare Tunnel reach private git servers and registries.

The admin surface is the dashboard's Cloud Agents section plus Enterprise settings: a network-access policy (Allow all / Default + allowlist / Allowlist only) that admins can lock org-wide, Runtime Secrets that are redacted from transcripts, tool output and commits, OIDC federation (issuer api.cursor.com, 5-minute RS256 tokens) so agents assume cloud roles without stored credentials, Protected Git Scopes and Repository Blocklist, and per-team toggles for agent summaries in Slack, Team follow-ups, Long running agents and Computer use. The default network policy is allow-all, and an Approval Agent can be configured to approve low-risk pull requests itself — both defaults an organisation should decide on deliberately.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Any paid plan can run Cloud Agents (Pro, Pro+, Ultra, Teams, Enterprise). Enterprise-only: network-policy lock, CMEK, PrivateLink / Cloudflare Tunnel, service accounts, Team Pools for Self-Hosted Machines, audit log and SIEM, OpenTelemetry export, Bugbot Admin API.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Cursor's hosted model providers under the team's Model Access Control; Auto-review in the cloud needs Claude 4.5 Haiku or GPT-5.4 Mini enabled. Self-Hosted Machines keep inference and planning in Cursor's cloud and send only the content the agent needs; workers connect outbound to api2.cursor.sh, api2direct.cursor.sh and the artifacts S3 bucket.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Nothing runs on the developer's device; the repository, secrets and environment live in the VM. Slack, GitHub and Linear see agent summaries and diffs (file paths included) unless the Display agent summary toggles are off; Slack Connect guests are governed by a separate external-channels toggle.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Privacy Mode always: Cursor never trains on code accessed by Cloud Agents or on their prompts and responses. Conversation state is retained indefinitely by default and deletable on demand; VM snapshots auto-delete after 90 days of inactivity; the runtime workspace is recycled when idle. Secrets are KMS-encrypted at rest.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Cloud Agents documentation (overview, security, secrets and network, identity, settings, private connectivity, self-hosted, automations, API).

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: Firecracker microVMs in a dedicated AWS account segregated from other Cursor services; one VM boundary per agent.

facts.label: Egress
facts.value: Published CIDR ranges per cluster (us3p, us4p, us5p) at cursor.com/docs/ips.json and a three-IP git egress proxy (184.73.225.134, 3.209.66.12, 52.44.113.131); the default network allowlist matches the desktop sandbox's defaults.

facts.label: Private connectivity
facts.value: AWS PrivateLink (endpoint service com.amazonaws.vpce.us-east-1.vpce-svc-054b15427d4bea2b7 for the api2.cursor.sh webhook path) or Cloudflare Tunnel for GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab Enterprise, Bitbucket Data Center and package registries; shared by Cloud Agents, Bugbot and backend services; Enterprise only, arranged via hi@cursor.com.

facts.label: Cursor Origin (excluded surface)
facts.value: Cursor's git forge, early beta since 2026-08-17 on Pro, Teams and Enterprise, with two-way GitHub PR sync; admins can disable Origin for the team from the dashboard, and a namespace must be claimed before enabling. Left out of the registry as code hosting rather than an agent runtime; treat repositories synced into Origin as a code-egress path to review.

facts.label: Vendor ownership
facts.value: SpaceX closed its acquisition of Anysphere (Cursor) on 2026-08-15; Cloud Agent infrastructure and subprocessors should be re-confirmed under the new owner.

riskNotes.note: A Cloud Agent reads repository content, PR comments, Slack threads and Linear issues as instructions and can browse the web; the vendor's stated mitigations are egress restriction, Runtime Secret redaction and the draft-PR gate. The default network policy is allow-all, so the first mitigation only exists once an admin locks Allowlist only.

The GitHub App is installed with eight permission categories including Administration; the agent can only reach repositories the triggering user could, but Automations run under the `cursor` account or a service account and Approval Agents can approve PRs on their own criteria — a machine identity approving machine-authored changes unless you keep approvals off.

OIDC tokens identify the whole run (cloud_agent_id, team_id, repo_urls) and any process on the VM can mint one from the local socket; scope IAM trust policies on aud and sub, not on the token existing. Egress IPs are shared across Cursor clusters, not per customer.

Agent summaries and diffs are posted into Slack, GitHub and Linear by default; conversation state persists indefinitely. Turn off Display agent summary in external channels, mark credentials as Runtime Secrets and set a deletion routine through the API.

Anyone on a paid plan can create Automations and any team member can create Private ones billed to their own account; Protected Git Scopes and admin promotion to Team Owned are the levers that bring them under the team's view.

controls.mechanism: Team SSO / SCIM; source-control connection by an account admin; Protected Git Scopes; Remote Control and Self-Hosted enablement under Dashboard → Cloud Agents

steps.title: Gate who can trigger agents
body: Members authenticate through the team's SSO; a Cursor account admin must connect GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps before any agent can clone, and the GitHub App can be installed on Selected repositories only.

steps.title: Lock your git organisation to your Cursor organisation
body: Enable Protected Git Scopes (needs GitHub org owner or admin) so only your Cursor teams can use those repositories with Cloud Agents and Bugbot.

steps.title: Decide on Remote Control and self-hosted workers
body: Under Cursor Dashboard → Cloud Agents → Self-Hosted enable or disable Remote Control for members; enabling it also enables the team's self-hosted worker access.

controls.mechanism: OIDC federation (issuer https://api.cursor.com, discovery /.well-known/openid-configuration, keys /keys); Enterprise service accounts

steps.title: Federate agent identity instead of storing keys
body: Create an IAM OIDC provider (or GCP WIF, Azure federated credential, Vault JWT auth) trusting https://api.cursor.com; agents mint 5-minute RS256 tokens from the VM socket with claims sub (user:<id> or service_account:<id>), aud, cloud_agent_id, team_id, repo_urls and agent_runtime=managed.

steps.title: Give automation its own identity
body: Create Enterprise service accounts under Dashboard → Settings → API Keys → Service Accounts; keys are shown once, can be rotated, and archiving the account revokes them; runs are visible to all team admins.

controls.note: The token identifies the run, not a process — any process with socket access can mint one.

controls.mechanism: Secrets tab per environment — Environment Variables, Runtime Secrets (redacted), Build Secrets (Docker build only); KMS at rest; OIDC short-lived tokens

steps.title: Mark credentials as Runtime Secrets
body: In the environment's Secrets tab store credentials as Runtime Secrets so values are replaced with [REDACTED] in tool results, transcript, commits and commit messages; use Build Secrets for values only the Docker build should see.

steps.title: Prefer federated tokens to stored keys
body: Replace long-lived cloud keys with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity against the Cursor OIDC issuer; tokens expire in five minutes.

controls.mechanism: CMEK / BYOK for Cloud Agent server-side encryption (Enterprise, via sales); AES-256 with per-agent keys; TLS 1.2+

steps.title: Map a customer-managed key
body: Ask your account team to map your KMS key for Cloud Agent data so you control rotation and access; per-agent session keys sit under it.

controls.mechanism: Dashboard → Cloud Agents and Automations lists; service accounts visible to admins; Bugbot repository list via /bugbot/repos

steps.title: Bring automations under the team
body: Admins can view, disable and promote automations to Team Owned (regenerates webhook keys and OAuth); Private and Team Visible automations otherwise bill and belong to their creator.

steps.title: Enumerate what Bugbot is enabled on
body: List repositories and settings with /bugbot/repos and set enabled or manualTriggerOnly per repository with /bugbot/repo/update.

controls.note: No approval workflow or declared-capability record; the lists are inventories, not a register with reconciliation.

controls.mechanism: Environment Builds and snapshots with version history; failed Builds do not replace the active one

steps.title: Pin environments to Builds
body: Define .cursor/environment.json (snapshot or build.dockerfile, install, start); a failed Build leaves agents on the last successful one and the Builds tab keeps the history.

controls.note: Rollout and rollback exist for the runtime image only; agent instructions and Automations have no versioning or staged release.

controls.mechanism: GitHub App scope (Selected repositories; access never wider than the triggering user); Protected Git Scopes; Repository Blocklist; Team feature settings (Long running agents, Computer use); per-automation tool enablement; MCP allowlist

steps.title: Scope repository reach
body: Install the GitHub App on Selected repositories, keep the Repository Blocklist for sensitive repos (glob patterns via /settings/repo-blocklists/repos), and rely on the rule that a Cloud Agent can only reach repositories the triggering user could.

steps.title: Switch off tools the team does not need
body: In Cloud Agent dashboard settings disable Computer use and Long running agents, and set Team follow-ups to Disabled or Service accounts only.

steps.title: Keep the MCP allowlist in force
body: The Enterprise MCP Configuration applies to cloud runs; Automations only get the tools (PRs, Slack, MCP, memory, computer use) you enable per automation.

controls.mechanism: Draft pull request as the review gate; Team follow-ups; Approval Agent approval toggle; Bugbot manualTriggerOnly

steps.title: Keep the PR gate human
body: Cloud Agents deliver draft PRs; branch protection in your forge is the deterministic gate. If you deploy PR Routing & Approval, leave approvals off unless you accept machine approval of low-risk PRs.

steps.title: Restrict who can steer a running agent
body: Set Team follow-ups to Disabled or Service accounts only so only the owner can add instructions from Slack or the web.

controls.note: There is no per-command approval inside a cloud run; the human step is at the pull request.

controls.mechanism: Egress allowlist, Runtime Secret redaction and draft-PR gating (vendor's listed mitigations); Team and Enterprise hooks run in cloud agents

steps.title: Apply the vendor's three mitigations
body: Lock Allowlist only egress, mark credentials as Runtime Secrets and keep the draft-PR gate; these are the documented prompt-injection mitigations for Cloud Agents.

steps.title: Run enterprise hooks in the cloud
body: Team hooks distributed from the dashboard and Enterprise-managed hooks also run in cloud agents, so beforeShellExecution and beforeSubmitPrompt checks apply there.

controls.note: No classifier over retrieved web, PR or Slack content; CVE-2026-61613 showed attacker web content reaching an unauthenticated agent endpoint inside the container (fixed 2026-03-31).

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence (trust portal, cursor.com/security, published egress ranges) consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

steps.title: Refresh the assessment for the hosted runtime
body: Record the dedicated-AWS-account and Firecracker isolation, the shared egress ranges, sub-processors, SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / ISO 42001 / AIUC-1 and the SpaceX ownership change.

controls.mechanism: Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export (cloud agent lifecycle, tool-call and token events); run stream via GET /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/stream; Automations run history

steps.title: Export lifecycle and tool events
body: Configure an OTLP/HTTP destination; logs include cloud agent lifecycle events, hook and plugin activation and builtin / MCP tool-call counts, with no prompt content, trace context or backfill.

steps.title: Capture transcripts at run time
body: Stream each run with the SSE endpoint and archive it; the API keeps run history per agent with pagination.

controls.note: No structured trace of reasoning steps, memory reads or handoffs is exported; Grok Bot's Action Recording does not apply to Cloud Agents.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise Audit Log with SIEM streaming; Admin API /teams/audit-logs

steps.title: Stream Cloud Agent audit events
body: The audit log records Cloud Agent environment creation, updates, restores and lifecycle changes, repository mappings, MCP authentication and Slack links; stream it to your SIEM or query /teams/audit-logs.

controls.note: Agent responses and generated code are explicitly not logged; retention and tamper-evidence are not stated on the page fetched.

controls.mechanism: Not offered — no admin-configurable content or topic filter
controls.note: Model Access Control chooses which models run and Anthropic applies its own cyber safeguards to Opus models (Enterprise groups can apply for the Cyber Verification Program to lift them), but there is no organisation-defined input or output guardrail.

controls.mechanism: Conversation state retained indefinitely, deletable on demand; agent archive / DELETE via API; Automations persistent memory as an opt-in tool

steps.title: Delete what you do not need
body: Archive or DELETE /v1/agents/{id} when work is merged; VM snapshots are removed after 90 days idle but conversation state is not.

steps.title: Keep memory off unless required
body: Enable the persistent-memory tool per automation only where the workflow needs it.

controls.note: No validation, quarantine or rollback of memory content; the control is deletion.

controls.mechanism: Not offered
controls.note: Bugbot and Security Agent analytics report findings and acceptance rates, which is outcome tracking rather than a scored evaluation harness; run your own.

controls.mechanism: Admin API and audit log as feeds into the organisation's governance platform
controls.note: Cursor has no catalogue with owners, risk tiers or intake workflow; the Admin API (members, model access, repo blocklists, audit logs) is the evidence source for one.

controls.mechanism: Usage-Based Pricing Settings (monthly team limit, admin-only changes); per-member spend limits (Enterprise) via /teams/user-spend-limit; API rate limits; one active run per agent

steps.title: Cap spend per team and member
body: Set the monthly team spending limit and, on Enterprise, individual limits per member from the dashboard or /teams/user-spend-limit; usage-based Cloud Agent, Bugbot and Automation runs draw from these pools.

controls.note: Limits are financial; there is no cap on tool-call depth or run duration beyond the Long running agents toggle.

controls.mechanism: POST /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/cancel; archive / delete agent; disable automation; archive service account (revokes keys); /teams/remove-member; Bugbot enabled=false

steps.title: Stop a run and revoke its identity
body: Cancel the run, then archive or delete the agent; archive the service account to revoke every key it holds while keeping the record for audit.

steps.title: Disable the integration
body: Admins can disable any automation from the dashboard and set enabled false per repository for Bugbot through /bugbot/repo/update.

controls.mechanism: Admin API endpoints (/teams/model-access/configuration, /teams/audit-logs, /settings/repo-blocklists/repos) polled by an SSPM product
controls.note: Cursor exposes configuration read APIs but ships no posture checks; the network-policy lock, Privacy Mode enforcement and Display-summary toggles are dashboard-only and must be verified manually.

advisories.title: CVE-2026-61613 — Cloud Agent browser sandbox escape: web content reaches an unauthenticated local agent endpoint (patched 2026-03-31)
CVE-2025-54135 CurXecute — Slack-sourced prompt injection writes MCP config (Cloud Agents read Slack threads and PR comments as input)

tools.name: Cursor

variants.name: Cursor IDE
Cursor CLI (agent)
Cursor for iOS / Web — Remote Control of a local agent

summary: Cursor is a VS Code-derived IDE and a companion CLI (installed as `agent`) that run an agent on the developer's machine with the developer's own credentials. Inference is never local: prompts and code context go to Cursor's backend (api2/api5.cursor.sh) and on to the model providers Cursor routes to, most under zero-data-retention terms, with Privacy Mode on by default for Enterprise teams and enforceable so members cannot switch it off. The Remote Control variant (Cursor 3.9.8+, iOS / web) moves only the agent loop to Cursor's cloud; terminal, file and git tool calls still execute on the developer's computer.

Admin control has two channels. MDM device policies (AllowedTeamId, AllowedExtensions, WorkspaceTrustEnabled, UpdateMode, ExtensionGalleryServiceUrl) ship as a macOS .mobileconfig, Windows ADMX or ~/.cursor/policy.json on Linux, and MDM can also drop ~/.cursor/permissions.json and an enterprise hooks.json. The Enterprise team dashboard pushes Run Mode policy, Model Access Control, MCP Configuration, Team Rules, Team hooks (synced every thirty minutes), Repository Blocklist, Protected Git Scopes, Browser Controls and .cursor Directory Protection; dashboard and hard-coded sandbox rules cannot be weakened by user or project files.

Two things leadership should hold onto. First, the docs are candid that the Auto-review classifier "can make mistakes" and that .cursorignore "is not a security boundary" — the hard controls are the sandbox policy, permissions.json deny rules and hooks that fail closed. Second, the local sandbox has had a steady run of escapes in 2026 (git hooks, .claude hook files, working-directory and symlink canonicalisation, privileged Docker containers, tampered venvs), all fixed by 3.0–3.1.2, plus an unfixed Windows C:\ProgramData\Cursor\hooks.json trust issue (CVE-2026-35603). Anysphere became a SpaceX subsidiary on 2026-08-15, which changes the vendor-risk file.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Free, Pro, Pro+, Ultra, Teams and Enterprise. Nearly every admin control on this entity is labelled Enterprise: SCIM, MDM policies, Model Access Control, MCP Configuration, Run Mode policy, Repository Blocklist, .cursor Directory Protection, Browser Controls, audit log, SIEM streaming, OpenTelemetry export, Admin API and service accounts.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Cloud-hosted only. The app talks to Cursor backends (*.cursor.sh, *.cursorapi.com, *.cursor-cdn.com, *.cursorvm.com; api2.cursor.sh for API, api5.cursor.sh for agent traffic) over TLS 1.2+ with certificate pinning, defaulting to HTTP/2 with an HTTP/1.1 SSE fallback; SSL inspection of these domains is documented as a cause of agent failures. Model Access Control (Team Settings → Models) fixes which providers and models a team may use and can block personal API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure, AWS Bedrock); Auto-review needs Claude 4.5 Haiku or GPT-5.4 Mini enabled for the team.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts and code context for every LLM request; the codebase index; MCP traffic to whatever servers are configured (terminal and MCP tools cannot be stopped by .cursorignore). Cloud Agents are the only feature that stores code, temporarily while a run executes. With Privacy Mode on, code is never used for training by Cursor or providers; models that keep inputs for provider-side safety review (Claude Fable 5/5.1) are disabled until an admin approves them.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Privacy Mode is on by default for Enterprise teams and enforceable org-wide; most models run under zero-data-retention agreements, ZDR does not apply when members bring their own API keys, and Claude Fable models retain inputs and outputs for Anthropic harm-prevention review (not training). Sub-processors are listed on the trust portal.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Enterprise documentation hub (identity, security hardening, LLM safety, models and integrations, compliance, network, OpenTelemetry, deployment patterns).

facts.label: Vendor ownership
facts.value: SpaceX closed its $60 billion all-stock acquisition of Anysphere (Cursor) on 2026-08-15; Cursor now operates as part of SpaceX and its Grok Bot product is co-branded with SpaceXAI. Reassess subprocessor, data-residency and contract terms accordingly.

facts.label: Certifications
facts.value: SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and AIUC-1; annual third-party pen test; no infrastructure in China; vulnerability reports to security-reports@cursor.com.

items.title: Identity and device management
body: SAML 2.0 SSO (password auth can be blocked), SCIM provisioning with group sync, and three dashboard roles. MDM policies for macOS and Windows cover Allowed Team IDs (blocks personal-account login on corporate devices), an Allowed Extensions allowlist (Cursor 2.1+) and Workspace Trust enforcement.

links.title: Cursor enterprise identity and access management

items.title: Privacy, model and MCP control
body: Privacy Mode is default-on for Enterprise teams and admins can enforce it so members cannot disable it; model access is set per team and per organisation group, and BYOK API keys can be blocked. MCP servers are governed by a dashboard allowlist with wildcard matching, per-server tool restrictions and per-server network policies, distributable to endpoints as ~/.cursor/permissions.json via MDM — admin settings take precedence over the local file and editor settings.

items.title: Agent run-mode policies and audit
body: Enterprise Run Mode policies (Cursor 3.6+) set the terminal posture — Auto-review, Allowlist, or Run Everything — and the docs are candid that the allowlist is best-effort, not a security boundary; hooks can scan prompts, block commands and redact secrets, and .cursorignore is likewise documented as not a boundary. Enterprise audit logs record admin and account events (explicitly not agent responses or generated code), stream to SIEM, and the Admin API exposes members, usage, spend, repo blocklists and model access.

riskNotes.note: Cursor's own mitigation is an LLM classifier (Auto-review) that the docs say can allow a call you would have blocked; the deterministic layer is sandbox.json plus permissions.json deny rules and hooks. Rules files, AGENTS.md and .cursor/* are instruction surfaces an attacker can reach through a repository (Rules File Backdoor), which is what .cursor Directory Protection and enforced Team Rules are for.

MCPoison (CVE-2025-54136) showed trust bound to an MCP server's name rather than its command; since 1.3 any change to an MCP configuration re-prompts. The Enterprise MCP allowlist matches command and URL patterns, so a pinned pattern is the only provenance check the vendor ships — the org must curate the Team Marketplace itself.

Run Everything mode removes every gate; the Enterprise Run Mode policy is the switch that takes it away from members. Five sandbox-escape advisories in 2026 mean the sandbox is a blast-radius reducer, not a guarantee; keep the fleet on 3.1.2 or later.

.cursorignore is a convenience filter that terminal and MCP tools bypass; beforeReadFile and beforeSubmitPrompt hooks (failClosed) and the sandbox's protected paths are the controls that hold. ZDR is lost the moment a member uses a personal API key, which Model Access Control can block.

The extension marketplace is a second supply chain inside the IDE: AllowedExtensions, Install Cooldown and ExtensionGalleryServiceUrl decide what can be installed; the .claude/settings.local.json hook escape (CVE-2026-48124) shows sibling-tool config files in a workspace are also executable surface.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise dashboard SSO (SAML 2.0) and SCIM 2.0; MDM policy AllowedTeamId / cursorAuth.allowedTeamId

steps.title: Turn on SSO and SCIM
body: Configure SAML 2.0 SSO (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, OneLogin) in the team dashboard and enable SCIM 2.0 provisioning with group sync; both require Enterprise and SCIM requires SSO.

steps.title: Pin corporate devices to your team
body: Set the MDM policy AllowedTeamId to the comma-separated list of authorised team IDs so personal accounts cannot sign in on managed devices; deploy via the shipped .mobileconfig (bundle com.todesktop.230313mzl4w4u92), the ADMX templates or ~/.cursor/policy.json on Linux.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise Run Mode policy (Auto-review / Allowlist / Run Everything); ~/.cursor/permissions.json via MDM; hooks.json beforeShellExecution / beforeMCPExecution with permission deny; CLI permissions.deny

steps.title: Set the Run Mode policy
body: In the Enterprise team dashboard set the run mode to Auto-review (default) or Allowlist and remove Run Everything; team settings take precedence over individual and project configuration.

steps.title: Distribute deterministic deny rules
body: Push ~/.cursor/permissions.json through MDM for terminal-command and MCP allow/deny lists; admin dashboard settings outrank the file, which outranks editor settings.

steps.title: Block at the hook boundary
body: Ship an enterprise hooks.json (/Library/Application Support/Cursor/hooks.json, /etc/cursor/hooks.json, C:\ProgramData\Cursor\hooks.json) with beforeShellExecution and beforeMCPExecution hooks returning permission deny; precedence is Enterprise → Team → Project → User and exit code 2 blocks.

steps.title: Lock the CLI the same way
body: In ~/.cursor/cli-config.json set permissions.allow / permissions.deny with Shell(), Read(), Write(), WebFetch() and Mcp(server:tool) rules; deny wins over allow.

controls.note: The docs state the Auto-review classifier can allow a call you would have blocked; only the deny rules, hooks and sandbox are deterministic.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence from cursor.com/security and trust.cursor.com consumed by the organisation's own TPRM platform

steps.title: Collect the vendor evidence
body: Pull SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001/42001, AIUC-1, the pen-test report and the sub-processor list from the trust portal; note the 2026-08-15 change of ownership to SpaceX and re-run the assessment.

controls.note: Cursor publishes evidence; the assessment cadence and reassessment trigger on ownership change must come from your TPRM tooling.

controls.mechanism: hooks.json beforeSubmitPrompt and beforeReadFile (Enterprise-managed, failClosed); .cursorignore as a convenience filter only

steps.title: Scan prompts and reads with hooks
body: Add beforeSubmitPrompt and beforeReadFile hooks in the enterprise or team hooks.json to scan for sensitive data and block or redact before content reaches the model; set failClosed on critical hooks.

steps.title: Do not rely on .cursorignore
body: Use .cursorignore for secrets and regulated trees, knowing terminal and MCP tools cannot be blocked by it and the docs call it a convenience feature, not a security boundary.

controls.note: No vendor-side content inspection or blocking policy exists; the docs point to endpoint DLP, hooks and third-party vendor APIs for centralised policy.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise MCP Configuration (server:tool allowlist patterns, per-server tool lists); ~/.cursor/permissions.json via MDM; CLI Mcp(server:tool) rules

steps.title: Allowlist MCP servers and tools
body: In the dashboard's MCP Configuration add command patterns for stdio servers and URL patterns for remote servers, then restrict each server's Tools field; patterns are server:tool, server:*, *:tool or *:*.

steps.title: Scope CLI tools per operation type
body: Use Shell(commandBase), Read(pathOrGlob), Write(pathOrGlob), WebFetch(domain) and Mcp(server:tool) entries in permissions.allow / permissions.deny; project-level .cursor/cli.json carries permissions only.

controls.mechanism: sandbox.json (type workspace_readwrite / workspace_readonly / insecure_none, additional paths, network policy); Run Mode sandboxing; team-admin policy layer cannot be weakened; CLI --sandbox and sandbox.mode

steps.title: Enable sandboxing in the Run Mode policy
body: Keep Auto-review or Allowlist with sandboxing enabled so non-allowlisted shell commands run in the sandbox that blocks protected files, writes outside approved paths and arbitrary network destinations.

steps.title: Set the sandbox policy
body: Configure ~/.cursor/sandbox.json (and per-repo .cursor/sandbox.json) with type, additionalReadwritePaths, additionalReadonlyPaths, disableTmpWrite and a network policy; merge order is per-user < per-repo < team-admin < hard-coded rules and the upper layers cannot be weakened.

steps.title: Sandbox the CLI
body: Set sandbox.mode and sandbox.networkAccess in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json or pass --sandbox <mode> in headless runs.

controls.note: Six sandbox-escape advisories were published Feb–Jul 2026 (git hooks, .claude hooks, working directory, symlinks, privileged Docker containers, tampered venvs); all fixed by 3.1.2. Treat the sandbox as blast-radius reduction.

controls.mechanism: Not offered for the local agent — it runs with the developer's own identity and credentials
controls.note: The local agent and CLI act as the signed-in user with whatever the shell can reach; Remote Control deliberately keeps credentials on the machine. Delegation controls (OIDC federation, Runtime Secrets, service accounts) exist only on Cloud Agents (toolCursorCloudAgents). Put scoped credentials in the developer's environment and use Runtime Secrets where the work can move to a Cloud Agent.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise .cursor Directory Protection; enforced Team Rules; Workspace Trust via MDM

steps.title: Protect the .cursor directory
body: Turn on .cursor Directory Protection in the team dashboard so agents cannot modify project settings (rules, MCP config, hooks) that persist across sessions.

steps.title: Restrict untrusted folders
body: Set the MDM policy WorkspaceTrustEnabled so untrusted folders open in restricted mode with AI features limited.

controls.note: Persistent state is project configuration rather than a memory store; there is no expiry, validation or rollback of agent memory.

controls.mechanism: Auto-review LLM classifier on non-allowlisted commands; beforeSubmitPrompt hooks; Browser Controls domain allowlist

steps.title: Keep Auto-review on
body: Auto-review runs allowlisted calls immediately, sandboxes what it can and routes the rest through an LLM classifier; enforce it from the Enterprise Run Mode policy.

steps.title: Limit what the browser tool can read
body: Define the Enterprise Browser Controls allowlist of approved domains so agents visiting other origins are blocked.

controls.note: There is no classifier on retrieved content or MCP tool output; the vendor's own language is that the classifier can make mistakes.

controls.mechanism: Team Settings → Models block on personal API keys; beforeReadFile hooks to redact secret files; Enterprise service-account keys (CURSOR_API_KEY) for the CLI

steps.title: Block personal model keys
body: In Team Settings → Models disable personal API keys so all usage routes through the team's included models and ZDR terms.

steps.title: Use service accounts for headless CLI
body: Create an Enterprise service account (Dashboard → Settings → API Keys → Service Accounts), store its one-time key as CURSOR_API_KEY in CI, rotate or archive it to revoke.

controls.note: No vault or just-in-time issuance for the secrets the local agent touches; .env files are ignored by default but not protected from terminal tools.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise MCP Configuration allowlist by command / URL pattern with per-server network modes; mandatory re-approval of any MCP config change (since 1.3); admin-curated Team Marketplaces

steps.title: Pin approved servers by pattern
body: Add each approved server's command or URL pattern to MCP Configuration and choose its network mode (Allow all, Allowlist, Deny all, No sandbox) for local servers.

steps.title: Curate a Team Marketplace
body: Publish approved MCP servers and plugins through Dashboard → Plugins, set installation mode (Default Off / Default On / Required) and turn off Allow Members to Publish.

controls.note: No content-hash pinning of tool definitions or rug-pull detection; the 1.3 fix re-prompts on configuration change, not on a server's own tool-list change.

controls.mechanism: Run Modes (Auto-review / Allowlist); MCP tools require approval by default; hooks can force ask/deny

steps.title: Remove Run Everything
body: Configure the Enterprise Run Mode policy so members cannot select Run Everything; Ask Every Time was deprecated in 3.5 in favour of Auto-review.

steps.title: Keep MCP approval prompts
body: Leave MCP tools outside the allowlist so Cursor asks for approval and shows arguments before each call.

controls.mechanism: Team Marketplaces (Dashboard → Plugins) and the MCP Configuration allowlist as the approved list; Active Sessions in Members

steps.title: Make the marketplace the register
body: Restrict marketplace visibility to Organization Groups via SCIM, set Required for mandated plugins and only allow admins to add marketplaces (Enterprise).

controls.note: There is no inventory of what is actually installed on endpoints or reconciliation against the allowlist.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise Audit Log (dashboard audit-log) with SIEM streaming; Admin API /teams/audit-logs; Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export

steps.title: Stream the audit log

tools.name: Grok Bot

variants.name: Grok Bot in Cursor (macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS)
Grok Bot in Slack

summary: Grok Bot gives each member named, persistent AI teammates ("Bots") that keep memory, files, browser sessions and preferences across sessions and run on a hosted cloud computer — a dedicated Firecracker microVM per user that every Bot belonging to that user shares. Bots sign into web apps, run shell commands, use the browser and terminal, message each other, learn routines by demonstration and rerun them on a schedule; work continues when the laptop or phone is closed. It launched in early beta on 2026-08-11 as a joint Cursor / SpaceXAI product and is bundled with paid Cursor and SuperGrok plans; Cursor operates it.

Inference is on Cursor's hosted providers and computers run in the United States only, with no per-customer data residency by default. Everything a Bot touches lives on the cloud computer, not the member's device; connector OAuth tokens stay on Cursor's backend and are never written to the computer, while login, two-factor and payment steps are handed back to the member. Egress uses shared static IP ranges across all Grok Bot customers; private networks are reached by installing the organisation's own VPN or zero-trust client through Team Setup.

Enterprise admins get an organisation-wide enable switch with Manage Group Access, Network Controls (four modes; teams without a policy default to allow-all, separate from the Cloud Agent policy), Team Setup manifests, Action Recording (off by default), Enforce Auto-review (off by default), computer management with termination, SCIM and audit logs of Bot control-plane events. Auto-review is the only action gate: it evaluates shell commands, plugin calls, computer use, automation writes and delegation, and the docs say it does not review all side effects such as memory writes.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Early beta from 2026-08-11 for Cursor Ultra, SuperGrok Heavy and Cursor Teams Premium, widened on 2026-08-21 to Pro+, Teams Standard and SuperGrok Plus (third-party reporting; Cursor's docs say paid individual plans, Cursor Teams or a linked SuperGrok subscription with weekly usage resets). All organisational controls are Enterprise only.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Cursor's hosted providers; Privacy Mode terms apply uniformly, including to Grok 4.5. Computers run in the United States today; custom residency requires the account team.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Nothing runs locally: files, browser sessions, memory and shell state live on the cloud computer; connector tokens stay on Cursor's backend and are never stored on the computer; internet egress uses shared ranges that identify Grok Bot traffic rather than your team.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Deletion follows the DPA — data is deleted or returned within 30 days of written direction after the service ends; Bot memory and files persist across sessions by design. Privacy Mode means code is not used for training.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Grok Bot documentation (overview, Teams and Enterprise, security, security FAQ, private networks, settings).

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: A dedicated Firecracker microVM with its own kernel, memory and virtual devices per user; all of one user's Bots share that computer, so separate credentials need separate Cursor user accounts.

facts.label: Vendor ownership
facts.value: Grok Bot is the first joint product after SpaceX's acquisition of Anysphere (closed 2026-08-15); the SpaceXAI docs mirror Cursor's and state that Anysphere operates the service.

riskNotes.note: A Bot browses arbitrary sites while signed into the member's SaaS accounts and reads Slack and group-chat messages as instructions; Auto-review is an LLM reviewer, and Network Controls default to allow-all until an Enterprise admin sets a policy.

Bots act with the member's connector tokens held on Cursor's backend and can delegate to Cloud Agents and subagents; the docs' guarantee is that a Bot never holds more access than its owner, so the member's own SaaS entitlements are the blast radius.

Persistent memory, files and browser sessions accumulate on a US-hosted computer that all of the user's Bots share; Action Recording is off by default, so what a Bot did with that data is not recorded unless an admin turns it on.

Grok Bot is bundled with individual paid plans, so members with personal accounts get it outside the organisation's switch; AllowedTeamId on managed devices and the org-wide switch with Manage Group Access are the containment.

controls.mechanism: Organisation-wide switch on the Grok Bot page with Manage Group Access; SSO and SCIM 2.0 (Enterprise)

steps.title: Decide who gets Bots
body: Use the organisation-wide switch on the Grok Bot dashboard page and Manage Group Access to enable it for specific groups; provision and deprovision through SCIM 2.0.

controls.mechanism: Named Bots bound to a member's identity; every action attributable to a named member; Bot creation and access changes in the audit log

steps.title: Keep Bots attributable
body: Bots inherit their owner's identity and can never hold more access than that member; use separate Cursor user accounts where workloads need distinct credentials.

controls.note: Bots have no credentials or keys of their own to inventory or rotate; identity governance is the member's.

controls.mechanism: Connector OAuth tokens held on Cursor's backend, never on the computer; login, 2FA and payment handed to the member

steps.title: Rely on backend-held connector tokens
body: Bots invoke connector tools without receiving OAuth tokens and tokens are never stored on the computer; credentials typed during browser sessions are outside this model, so hand those steps to the member.

controls.note: No vault or just-in-time issuance for secrets the Bot uses inside its shell or browser sessions.

controls.mechanism: Not stated on the Grok Bot pages fetched
controls.note: The Cloud Agent CMEK offer is documented as Cloud Agent data; the Grok Bot security, FAQ and Teams pages do not say whether customer-managed keys cover Bot computers. Ask the account team before relying on it.

controls.mechanism: Computer management (look up any member's computer, creation and last-active times); audit log of Bot creation and member access changes

steps.title: Inventory computers and Bots
body: Organisation admins can look up any member's computer, see when it was created and last active, and read Bot creation and access-change events in the audit log.

controls.note: No approval step or declared-capability record per Bot.

controls.mechanism: Not offered
controls.note: Team Setup manifests push install scripts to every computer but no versioning, staged release or rollback of Bots, routines or manifests is documented.

controls.mechanism: Network Controls (four modes, team allowlist); Team Setup; Auto-review Ask first / Allow automatically rules; Bot access bounded by its owner

steps.title: Set a network policy
body: Pick one of the four Network Controls modes; teams without a policy default to allow-all, and the policy is separate from Cloud Agent network settings and applies when a computer is created or recreated.

steps.title: Write Auto-review rules
body: Ask first rules always stop matching actions and Allow automatically rules let them proceed when the reviewer finds no safety concern; admins set team rules and members may only add stricter personal ones.

controls.mechanism: Enforce Auto-review (Enterprise, off by default); Ask first rules; login, 2FA and payment always handed to the member

steps.title: Enforce Auto-review
body: Turn on Enforce Auto-review on the Grok Bot page so members cannot switch the reviewer off; it evaluates shell commands, plugin calls, computer use, automation writes and delegation and can allow, require approval or deny.

controls.note: The docs state Auto-review does not review all side effects, such as memory writes.

controls.mechanism: Auto-review LLM reviewer over actions; Network Controls allowlist

steps.title: Combine the reviewer with an allowlist
body: Enforce Auto-review and set a team allowlist in Network Controls so an injected instruction cannot both act and exfiltrate.

controls.note: No classifier on the web pages or messages a Bot reads.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence (Cursor trust portal, ISO 27001/42001, DPA) consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

steps.title: Assess the new surface
body: Record US-only hosting, shared egress ranges, the DPA's 30-day deletion term, the SpaceXAI co-branding and Anysphere's ISO 27001 / 42001 certifications.

controls.mechanism: Action Recording (Enterprise, off by default) plus OpenTelemetry Export tagged cursor.surface=grok_bot

steps.title: Record Bot actions
body: Turn on Action Recording on the Grok Bot page to capture Bot actions including scrubbed shell commands, then enable OpenTelemetry Export so shell, browser, tool-call and computer-use events reach your collector.

steps.title: Export the events
body: Configure Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export; Grok Bot actions arrive as logs with no prompt content.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise audit log covering Grok Bot control-plane events; SIEM streaming

steps.title: Stream Grok Bot audit events
body: Audit logs cover admin, security and authentication events plus Bot creation, member access changes, Team Setup manifests, MCP authentication, Slack account links and routines.

controls.mechanism: Not offered
controls.note: No organisation-defined content or topic filter; Auto-review gates actions, not content.

controls.mechanism: Per-user microVM; admin computer termination; separate user accounts for separate credentials

steps.title: Terminate a computer to reset state
body: Organisation admins can terminate any member's computer; provision separate Cursor user accounts where workloads must not share memory, files or browser sessions.

controls.note: Memory persists by design and Auto-review does not evaluate memory writes; there is no validation, expiry or rollback.

controls.mechanism: Not offered
controls.note: No evaluation harness for Bots or routines.

controls.mechanism: Audit log and computer management as feeds to the organisation's governance platform
controls.note: No catalogue with owners, risk tiers or intake; Bots are created by members without an approval workflow.

controls.mechanism: Weekly usage allowances per plan; Cursor team spend limits

steps.title: Cap spend through the team
body: Grok Bot usage draws on plan allowances that reset weekly with on-demand billing beyond them; team and per-member spend limits in the Cursor dashboard bound the cost.

controls.note: No limit on routine frequency, action count or task duration is documented.

controls.mechanism: Organisation-wide switch; Manage Group Access; computer termination by admins; SCIM deprovisioning

steps.title: Stop a Bot or the whole feature
body: Terminate the member's computer from computer management, remove the group in Manage Group Access, or flip the organisation-wide switch off.

controls.mechanism: Dashboard-only settings verified manually or through an SSPM product
controls.note: Network Controls, Enforce Auto-review and Action Recording have no documented API; posture checks must read the dashboard.
